# dsh-remote-web-ui · Mobile & Cross-Device Remote Web Control for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) English | [中文](README.zh.md)

   

Mobile & Cross-Device Remote Web Control for DeepSeek Harness (DSH)
Instant QR Pairing · Cross-Device PC Access · Mobile Touch Gestures · Cloudflare Tunnels · Secure Device Session

> Seamless remote access for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Web GUI and desktop client sharing the **exact same interface**: pair an iPhone, Android smartphone, tablet, or another computer from the QR code next to settings. Both ends run the authentic official Web GUI — phones receive an injected portrait touch layer while remote computers enjoy the complete desktop workbench. Access is guarded by expiring pairing tokens and revocable sessions. Built-in LAN binding and optional Cloudflare quick tunnels enable effortless external access with persistent hostnames. This package is an official external plugin for DeepSeek Harness (DSH), structured as a cordis bundle: the host half manages pairing tokens, device sessions, `/api/pair` routes, the gated `/remote` channel, and LAN binding; the browser half renders the remote access trigger, QR pairing modal, live device roster, settings card, and mobile portrait touch adaptation. ## What it does - **Entry**: a phone icon beside the settings button in both the expanded sidebar and the narrow rail; its tooltip and accessible label say "Remote access". - **Panel**: "Remote access" title, a "Pair a device" card with the status area ("Waiting for a device" + status badge), a large QR code, the pairing link with its copy button, Stop / Refresh QR actions, and the authorized-device roster (a saved device name that falls back to the User-Agent-derived label, online/offline, last active time, per-device rename and unpair, and a merge action for rows sharing one User-Agent). Credential-bearing device ids and raw User-Agent values are never rendered. Both the phone and the PC use the same time-limited link: until it expires or the QR is refreshed, that link can pair several devices, each with its own device session. - **Phone side**: scanning the QR binds the phone with a time-limited token and reloads into the **official Web GUI** — there is no second interface to drift from. While the phone is in portrait, the plugin injects a touch-adaptation layer over the running UI (see "The mobile adaptation layer" below). The accept chain is cookieless (`/pair-accept` → `/pair-app`): the plugin itself serves the official shell, so the phone needs no harness browser-auth cookie at all. A reopen service worker (https origins) then owns later navigations to `/` from history, bookmarks, or tab restore, so the phone reopens straight into the app instead of a 401 dead end (see Security model). - **PC side**: the same link opens the full desktop Web GUI on another computer over the gated `/remote` channel; unpaired PCs see a guided blocking page (with a manual pair-token input) and no workspace data behind it. - **Security**: one active token at a time (a refresh invalidates the old link; the link stays re-usable within its expiry window so a scan handed between browsers can complete pairing; it expires). 停止 revokes every paired device and the current token — the `/remote` channel cuts them off on their next request. Pairing is this plugin's access control for the `/remote` channel; the web server keeps its loopback bind, so a LAN browser reaches the app through this plugin's gated `/remote` gateway (the client moves its transport there) rather than the native `/api`, which the harness Host fence answers with 403 for a LAN authority (see Security model). Loopback (127.0.0.1) keeps using `/api` directly, and so does a page an application on this machine delivered — the desktop shell's `dsh-app://app/` or a `file:` page — because a pairing link is reachable only over the network. A paired device is a **full-control credential** (see Security model). - **LAN access toggle (runtime forwarder)**: the settings card starts a forwarder instead of touching any file. The web server keeps its loopback bind, and the forwarder listens on this machine's LAN IPv4 address at the same port, re-issuing every request — HTTP and WebSocket upgrades alike — to `127.0.0.1:`. `--host`/`--port` keep their ordinary meaning, so an explicit `dsh web --host ` still works and the forwarder then yields the port. The toggle applies while the process runs: no restart, no profile edit. When this machine has no LAN IPv4 address the forwarder stays off and the card says so. It maintains the matching host firewall rule (Windows Defender via netsh; Linux firewalld/ufw/iptables; other platforms report the firewall as unmanaged) and shows the live bind, the reachable LAN URLs, the forwarder state (`forward { listening, host, port, reason, error }`) beside the host's own `localBindHost`, and the firewall state. - **Live status**: the desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; an `/api` posture probe reports any host whose `/api` fence the SDK leaves open, and the auto-tunnel state appears on the panel while the tunnel is starting. - **Self-update lives next door**: the one-click family update is its own plugin (`dsh-update`, the same sidebar foot seat), so turning remote access off — or disabling this plugin — never removes the update trigger. - **Desktop foot row**: on the wide sidebar the footer-action occupants share the official Settings trigger's line instead of stacking above it, so no single control owns a full-width row; any other foot block (the usage glance card, another plugin's) keeps a full row above them, and the 56px rail keeps the shell's stacked foot. ## The mobile adaptation layer The official desktop layout already auto-collapses the sidebar below 1024px. On top of that, while the viewport is portrait + coarse pointer + narrower than 1100px the plugin injects: - a CSS sheet keyed on CSS-Modules **semantic suffixes** (`[class$="_composerSeat"]`) so the selectors survive official rebuilds that only change hashes: 44px touch targets on the collapsed rail, 16px inputs (prevents iOS focus zoom), safe-area padding for the composer, compact type for the message list and sidebar, a column layout for the settings modal, and a full-width PlanReview card; - a **draggable whale button** as the entry to the collapsed sidebar (position persisted; wired to the official `ctx.layout.toggleSidebar()`), hidden while the sidebar is expanded; - **gestures**: left-swipe collapses the sidebar, right-swipe in the conversation opens it; long-pressing a session row opens the same action menu as the desktop ellipsis; tapping a session row or anywhere outside the sidebar collapses it again; - **input behavior for touch**: Enter only inserts a newline (send goes through the send button), programmatic composer focus is suppressed (no spurious keyboards), and official tooltip bubbles are hidden because taps leave them stuck; - **mobile plugin scope**: while the layer is active, the right-hand details column and the desktop-oriented tool surfaces (SSH terminal, skill explorer, task board, git graph, pet, usage) are hidden - keyed on the L2 semantic roots (`data-dsh-plugin`), so ownership stays with the declaring plugin and class churn cannot resurrect them. These are render suppressions; the client bundles still load. Activation also closes the details panel through the official `ctx.layout.closeDetails()`. - a **manual opt-out**: `sessionStorage.dsh-remote-force-desktop = 1` disables the whole layer; landscape, desktop, and wide viewports are never touched. The paired remote desktop also runs in **host mode**: on this harness line the "configuration plane is local" behavior is a client-side branch on `connection.isLoopback`, and the channel boot script installs the transport hook (`__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost = true`) before any boot entry. Host mode is **server-granted**: the hook is installed only when the device-gated app landing (`/pair-app`) published the grant marker ahead of the boot patch, so a shell served to an unpaired browser — a fence-open deployment — never poses as the machine owner. Settings, credentials, agent presets, and deliverables therefore work on the phone exactly as on the desktop — every call still rides the gated `/remote` channel. Three control planes stay physically local: `/api/pair/*`, `/api/update/*`, and `/api/plugin-manager/*`. ## Requirements - A DSH installation whose `dsh` CLI supports profiles (`dsh --profile`, `dsh plugin`) — the profile/bundle mechanism this package rides on. - For LAN use, either flip the **局域网访问** toggle in the settings card — it listens at once on this machine's current LAN IPv4 address at the web server's port, so after a network change flip it off and on again — or start with `dsh web --host `. A wildcard `--host 0.0.0.0` works only on a host that still accepts it; DSH 0.2.1-rc.2 and later refuses it outright. With the default `127.0.0.1` bind the panel shows an explicit explanation instead of a dead QR code — unless a public base URL is configured (see "Remote access over the internet" below), which makes the QR reachable from anywhere without rebinding, after which a phone on the same network is moved off the tunnel onto the LAN origin by the landing page. The panel's mint/stop endpoints are loopback-only by design: a desktop browser opened at the LAN URL sees a "配对面板仅限本机使用" banner. - For the one-click public tunnel (`autoTunnel`), the `cloudflared` platform binary ships with the package (its postinstall downloads it; a runtime download covers installers that skip postinstall scripts). No user-side tooling, account, or domain is needed. - The same binary also powers the fixed-hostname named-tunnel mode (`tunnelToken`): the public hostname never changes, so a paired phone keeps its bookmark and its pairing cookie across restarts and never re-pairs. ## Install Install the family aggregate package `@linxin666/dsh-web-all` (all plugins and skins in one) or this plugin alone: ```sh # Recommended: install directly from npm dsh plugin --profile web add @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui@latest # Or from the repository (development loop) git clone https://github.com/zhu1090093659/dsh-web.git cd dsh-web pnpm install && pnpm -r build dsh plugin --profile web add link:$(pwd)/packages/dsh-remote-web-ui ``` Restart the profile (`dsh web`), then open the phone icon in the sidebar foot. The plugin's `cordis.patch.yml` inserts the single plugin row that mounts both halves. > `github:/` installs work for a standalone repo whose package sits at the root (the `prepare` script builds `lib/` during install; pnpm ≥10 blocks that until you copy the printed key into the profile's `pnpm-workspace.yaml` `allowBuilds` and re-run). Monorepo subpackages use the `link:` form above. ## Use 1. Open the settings card (设置 → Web 插件 → 远程访问) and flip **局域网访问** on; the card shows the live bind, the forwarder state beside the host's own `localBindHost`, the firewall state, and the reachable LAN URLs, and it says why the LAN entry is off when this machine has no LAN address. The forwarder starts and stops at once, with no restart: after a network change, flip the toggle off and on again so it follows the machine's new address. 2. Start `dsh web`, click the phone icon, and the panel mints a fresh time-limited QR. 3. Scan with the phone (or open the copied link): the device pairs and boots the **official Web GUI** served cookieless by the plugin (`/pair-accept` → `/pair-app`), which reloads into `/`. When the link names the public base, the landing page also probes the advertised LAN origins (one short no-cors request to `/pair-ping` per candidate) and moves the phone to the first one that answers, remembering the decision for the session: the public page it was served from stays usable throughout, so the probe never blocks pairing, and a phone that is not on that network simply stays where it is. On a phone, the portrait adaptation layer is already active — same layout as the desktop, same live state. Later reopens from history or a bookmark go straight back into the app (https origins; see Security model). 4. **To pair a PC instead**: copy the same link and open it in a browser on the other computer. After the same round trip the full Web GUI runs there over the gated `/remote` channel; unpaired PCs see the guided blocking page and no data. One active token pairs one device; mint a fresh QR for the next device. 5. The desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; the device roster lists the paired devices with per-device 取消配对, and 停止 revokes everything. 6. Configure pairing lifetime, device limits, the LAN fence policy (`requirePairingForLan`), the public base URL, the auto tunnel, the stable-hostname relay, and the named-tunnel token in the same settings card. Which network the pair traverses needs no choice: the QR link names the public base and the landing page moves a same-network phone to a LAN origin by itself. If that probe ever misjudges, pin it with the patch-only `pairingSource` key (`auto` | `public` | `lan`); the card carries no control for it, so a save from the card leaves it alone. ## Remote access over the internet (tunnels) A tunnel process restart — most often a mobile network dropping and reconnecting — used to drop the public host from the pairing fence the moment the tunnel left `running`, so the address still printed in the QR code answered 403, including on the deliberately public `/api/pair/status` (issue #1547). A named tunnel's fixed hostname and a registered relay origin never change, so both now stay trusted throughout the reconnect; a quick tunnel's previous host stays trusted for a 60 s grace window, because the edge may still be delivering a connection the phone already opened, and is dropped only if the tunnel has not come back by then. ### One-click public tunnel (recommended) Set **自动公网隧道** (autoTunnel) in the settings card. The plugin runs its own Cloudflare quick tunnel (`cloudflared` ships with the package), feeds the minted public URL into the QR base and the pairing fence dynamically, and keeps the posture probe informed — a phone anywhere can pair at any time. The manual public address and the named-tunnel token below are ignored while this is on. The minted hostname is ephemeral and changes on every `dsh web` restart — the stable-hostname relay below keeps the phone's origin fixed across those restarts. A host that dies without tearing its tunnel down leaves the `cloudflared` child running, so each start reaps the child it recorded (pid plus an exactly matching command line) and never a process it did not start itself. ### Stable-hostname relay (default on; pair once across restarts) While the quick tunnel runs, the plugin additionally registers its current tunnel URL with the dsh-market relay registry and rebuilds the QR on a fixed origin — `https://.dsh-market.com` — minted once per profile and stored under `$DSH_HOME/remote-web-ui-registry/`. The hostname never changes, so the phone's bookmark and its pairing cookie keep working across `dsh web` restarts with no Cloudflare account, no dashboard, and no domain of your own. - Registration is secret-authenticated: the plugin mints a 256-bit secret next to the identity and re-syncs the mapping on every tunnel start (crash restarts included) with capped backoff. If the registry is unreachable, the QR falls back to the raw quick URL for that session and the panel says so. - A phone opening the stable origin while the instance is offline sees an explicit "instance offline — refresh in a moment, no re-pairing needed" page instead of a dead link. - Turn **固定域名中继** (relay) off in the settings card to keep the deployment entirely on the ephemeral origin; the registry row is removed at once. Trust note: relayed traffic transits the dsh-market edge (a Cloudflare Worker operated by the package author) — see Security model. - The relay control plane is additive: whenever the relay is on and the web server port is bound, the plugin claims a named-tunnel lease from `https://dsh-market.com/api/relay/claim` — the worker finds or creates the tunnel named `dsh-relay-`, writes its ingress (catch-all rule included) and an exact proxied CNAME, and hands back that instance's own tunnel token. A lease an operator flipped to the bridge transport converges nothing in the account: that claim creates no tunnel, no ingress and no CNAME, sends no Cloudflare API call at all, keeps only the hostname and the bridge grant, and answers no `tunnel` block — the bridge's data plane is the instance's own Durable Object, so there is nothing to build and nothing to count against the account's 1 000-tunnel quota. The plugin then runs a named connector on the same hostname beside the quick connector; the `mode` the control plane answers names the one the phone is served from, so neither the switch nor its rollback needs a plugin restart. A failed claim is not fatal: the quick tunnel and the origin the registry already gave the phone keep serving, and the claim retries with capped backoff (`502` carries `retryAfterMs`). Turning the toggle off only `release`s the lease (the tunnel and the DNS record stay, so re-enabling is instant); only an explicit `retire` or the 90-day idle cron recovers the source. - The bridge transport rides the same lease: the plugin dials `wss://dsh-market.com/api/relay/bridge?id=` with the lease secret in the `Authorization` header and serves every bridged request and phone WebSocket from that one socket, forwarding the public origin as `Host` and never the loopback authority it dials. It idles while the control plane answers `mode=quick`; with no connector attached the Worker falls back to the quick path inside the same request and marks the answer `x-relay-fallback: no-connector`. Because the claim is the only answer that carries the bridge grant, it does not wait for a quick tunnel: an instance served over the bridge reaches its object with `autoTunnel` off. The connector keeps its state in `$DSH_HOME/remote-web-ui-relay-bridge.json` — state, instance, endpoint, local upstream and the last dial error — so a connector that never attached is readable without the host log. ### Fixed-hostname named tunnel (bring your own domain) The relay above already fixes the phone's origin on a shared dsh-market subdomain. A Cloudflare named tunnel is the alternative for deployments that want a hostname on **their own** domain: its public hostname is permanent, so the phone's bookmark and its pairing cookie keep working across `dsh web` restarts — pair once, never again (until the session idles past `idleExpireMs`). 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard create a Tunnel and map a public hostname — e.g. `dsh.example.com` — to `http://127.0.0.1:3080` (the port `dsh web` listens on). 2. Copy the tunnel's token and paste it into **固定域名隧道令牌** (tunnelToken) in the settings card. 3. Set the same hostname as **公网地址** (publicBaseUrl). The token does not carry the hostname, so without this step the tunnel stays off and a warning names the missing piece. The plugin then runs `cloudflared tunnel run --token` with the same lifecycle management as the quick tunnel: the binary ships with the package, unexpected exits restart with backoff, a running tunnel's public URL is probed every 60 s and two consecutive failures mint a fresh tunnel through that same restart path, and the posture probe audits the `/api` fence for the fixed host. The token is stored as a settings secret and read back redacted. The auto quick tunnel takes precedence while it is on. A `running` tunnel is not a terminal state: a connector that lost its Cloudflare edge registration keeps its process and its metrics port alive while the minted hostname stops resolving, so the plugin used to report `running` indefinitely and the relay kept forwarding the phone to the dead address (Cloudflare 530 / Error 1016) instead of the relay's offline page (issue #1723). The readiness watchdog now treats a public URL that stops answering — DNS failure, refused connection, or a Cloudflare 5xx such as 530 — as a dead tunnel after two consecutive probes, and the ordinary backoff restart mints a new URL and re-registers the relay. An unauthenticated `401`/`403` answer still counts as alive, because that is a healthy round trip to a harness that has not been paired yet. ### Manual tunnels (bring your own) Expose the local port with any tunnel and set **公网地址** (publicBaseUrl), e.g.: ```sh # 1. Expose the local port (whatever dsh web is listening on): cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:3080 # prints something like: https://xxxx-xxxx-xxxx.trycloudflare.com # 2. Start dsh web as usual. Do not add --trusted-host for the tunnel # domain unless you intentionally want the SDK to trust that host for # /api. Keep the LAN bind off if only tunnel access is wanted. ``` Then set the printed URL as 公网地址. The QR link is built from it, and the plugin's pairing fence accepts the tunneled authority. The posture probe keeps auditing which `/api` authorities the SDK fence leaves open. ## Development Work from this repository (no sibling checkout needed): ```sh cd dsh-web export NPM_TOKEN='' # only if private @deepseek-ai auth is still required pnpm install pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui run build pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui test pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui run typecheck ``` The peer APIs come from the official NPM SDK: every `@deepseek-ai/*` package used here is declared in devDependencies (0.2.1-rc.3 cohort), and TypeScript/Vitest resolve types straight from node_modules — no DSH source checkout is required. The consumer-side `prepare` build (`tsdown.prepare.config.ts`) transpiles without type checking, so git installs work without any harness checkout either. ## Checks ```sh pnpm run typecheck pnpm test pnpm run build ``` ## Harness contract dependencies Pinned to the 0.2.1-rc.3 line; the seams this build relies on: - **`sidebar.footer.action` foot seat** (the 0.1.7 shell composition): the sidebar declares and renders the seat the remote entry occupies. - **`ctx.layout.toggleSidebar()`** (packages/client/ui-layout): the whale button expands the collapsed sidebar through the official panel-action face. - **`ctx.connection.authenticatedUrl()`** (packages/client/connection): the sanctioned launch-token seam the proxy redeems once for its inner credential (`src/inner-auth.ts`), so re-issued `/api` calls satisfy the harness browser-auth check. - **`__DSH_FILE_UPLOAD__`** (file-upload client hooks): the optional pre-Cordis transport the upload service reads once at construction. The remote boot patch publishes it so background uploads stay on the rewritten main-thread fetch instead of a Web Worker that escapes the channel (issue #1580). - **`__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost`** (client-connection transport hooks): the host-mode flip for paired remote desktops. It is installed only when the device-gated app landing published the `__DSH_REMOTE_HOST_GRANT__` marker ahead of the boot patch, so the flip is server-granted rather than asserted from the origin. There is no host-side per-method privilege pin on this line — the configuration plane branches on `connection.isLoopback` in the client — and no `api/gate` waterfall either (the gate listener stays mounted for deployments that gain the seam; pairing enforcement lives on this plugin's own `/remote` channel). - **Web server bind ownership**: the profile's `- id: webserver` row belongs to the official bundle and this plugin never writes it — same-id patch rows replace a row's config wholesale, and the user patch layer cannot evaluate `webStartup`-dependent `!!js` expressions reliably, so the row keeps `host: !!js ctx.webStartup.host ?? '127.0.0.1'` and `--host`/`--port` reach it. LAN reachability is runtime state instead: the forwarder in `src/lan-forward.ts` listens on the LAN interface at the web server's actual port and re-issues to `127.0.0.1` on the same port. The fence helpers (`isTrustedApiRequest` / `isLoopbackHostname`) are reimplemented locally in `src/gate.ts` / `src/routes.ts`: the connection plugin stopped exporting them, so the pairing routes carry their own copy scoped to the literals the QR links advertise. The loopback question is split in two there: `isLoopbackUpstream` (loopback socket and Host, forwarding headers ignored) only decides whether a Host can be answered at all, while `isLoopbackClient` (no forwarding header) decides who receives a credential or the desktop payload. The shared copy in `shared/host/loopback.ts` keeps `isLoopbackRequest` refusing every forwarded request and adds `isForwardedLoopbackRequest` for the narrower shape a route family may admit behind its own default-off switch. ## Manual E2E: LAN pairing round trip The unit/component specs cover the route family, the gate, the channel, the LAN forwarder with its status frame, and the adaptation layer, but the pairing loop involves a real browser on a non-loopback origin. Repeat this after any change to the wire contract or the connection loop: 1. Start an isolated instance: `DSH_HOME=/tmp/dsh-qa dsh --profile web --no-open --port 3191`; open the card at `http://127.0.0.1:3191`, flip **局域网访问** on, and confirm the card reports the forwarder listening on the machine's LAN IPv4 at 3191. 2. Open the **loopback** URL (`http://127.0.0.1:3191`) in a browser: the phone icon sits in the sidebar foot; the panel mints a QR whose link is `/pair-accept?pair=`. With a public base configured the link names that origin instead — reachable from anywhere — and the landing does the network choice described under **Use**. 3. In a second tab under mobile emulation (390x844, touch) open that link: the chain `/pair-accept → /pair-app?grant= → /` on an https origin, ending at `/pair-app` instead over plain-HTTP LAN, sets the device cookie, spends the grant, serves the patched official shell, and boots the UI — `document.body.classList` carries `dsh-remote-portrait`, the adaptation stylesheet and the whale button exist, and `__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost` is `true`. The settings surface renders host data (host mode), not a memory mirror. In an https deployment the shell also registers the reopen service worker (`/pair-app.sw.js`); reloading `/` in that tab boots the app instead of the harness 401. Over plain-HTTP LAN the same tab reloads `/pair-app` and boots the app from the pairing cookie instead. 4. The desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; a LAN-origin desktop page instead shows the 配对面板仅限本机使用 banner and opens no status stream. 5. 停止 on the desktop cuts the device off: its next request 403s with `unpaired` (the fence page offers the manual pair-token input). The public path is the same round trip through a tunnel (see "Remote access over the internet"): loopback mint → device opens the public QR URL → accept → official UI, and when the advertised LAN origin actually answers (check with `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://:/pair-ping`, expecting 204) the landing replaces itself with `http://:/pair-app?grant=` and the UI boots from the LAN origin. Re-scanning the public QR within the same session lands on the public source again, because the decision records the failed switch. Only `publicBaseUrl` (plugin config) names the tunneled host; `--trusted-host` is not part of this pairing flow. The desktop panel still opens at `http://127.0.0.1`. ## Security model - **Pairing is the access control for the `/remote` channel, unconditionally**: every request must carry a live paired-device cookie, enforced before any bytes are forwarded. A missing or revoked session receives HTTP 403 with a JSON rejection carrying `error.code: "unpaired"`; the browser's `EventSource` API exposes only the stream failure, not that response body. This gate does **not** follow `requirePairingForLan`: the channel re-issues every call with the process's own browser-auth credential, so admitting an unpaired caller would hand out that authority. The LAN policy governs the plain `/api` surface only and can never widen the channel (issue #1665). - **The channel carries the process's own inner credential.** The harness browser-auth cookie is authority-bound (minted for the exact `host:port` a browser visited) and has no loopback exemption, so a proxied re-issue to `127.0.0.1` cannot reuse a device's cookie. The plugin therefore redeems its own launch token once — the same exchange a first browser visit performs — and attaches that cookie to re-issued requests. The credential is only ever exercised behind the pairing gate above; 停止/取消配对 immediately stop exercising it. - **The channel forwards the caller's own request headers, and keeps only what it owns (issue #1925).** A plugin may authenticate its own calls with a header of its own — `x-dsh-im-connect-client` on `@michengai/dsh-im-connect`'s `/sessions/ensure` is the reported case — so the re-issue no longer rebuilds the request from a fixed allowlist: every header is forwarded except the ones this channel owns. It rewrites `host` to the loopback authority, replaces the caller's cookie with the process's inner credential, synthesizes `sec-fetch-site: same-origin`, and drops `origin`/`referer`, the whole browser fetch-metadata family (`sec-*`), hop-by-hop headers (including the ones the caller nominates in its own `Connection` header), the forwarding marks (`x-forwarded-*`, `cf-connect

# dsh-remote-web-ui · Mobile & Cross-Device Remote Web Control for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) English | [中文](README.zh.md)

   

Mobile & Cross-Device Remote Web Control for DeepSeek Harness (DSH)
Instant QR Pairing · Cross-Device PC Access · Mobile Touch Gestures · Cloudflare Tunnels · Secure Device Session

> Seamless remote access for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Web GUI and desktop client sharing the **exact same interface**: pair an iPhone, Android smartphone, tablet, or another computer from the QR code next to settings. Both ends run the authentic official Web GUI — phones receive an injected portrait touch layer while remote computers enjoy the complete desktop workbench. Access is guarded by expiring pairing tokens and revocable sessions. Built-in LAN binding and optional Cloudflare quick tunnels enable effortless external access with persistent hostnames. This package is an official external plugin for DeepSeek Harness (DSH), structured as a cordis bundle: the host half manages pairing tokens, device sessions, `/api/pair` routes, the gated `/remote` channel, and LAN binding; the browser half renders the remote access trigger, QR pairing modal, live device roster, settings card, and mobile portrait touch adaptation. ## What it does - **Entry**: a phone icon beside the settings button in both the expanded sidebar and the narrow rail; its tooltip and accessible label say "Remote access". - **Panel**: "Remote access" title, a "Pair a device" card with the status area ("Waiting for a device" + status badge), a large QR code, the pairing link with its copy button, Stop / Refresh QR actions, and the authorized-device roster (a device name inferred from User-Agent, online/offline, last active time, per-device unpair). Credential-bearing device ids and raw User-Agent values are never rendered. Both the phone and the PC use the same time-limited link: until it expires or the QR is refreshed, that link can pair several devices, each with its own device session. - **Phone side**: scanning the QR binds the phone with a time-limited token and reloads into the **official Web GUI** — there is no second interface to drift from. While the phone is in portrait, the plugin injects a touch-adaptation layer over the running UI (see "The mobile adaptation layer" below). The accept chain is cookieless (`/pair-accept` → `/pair-app`): the plugin itself serves the official shell, so the phone needs no harness browser-auth cookie at all. A reopen service worker (https origins) then owns later navigations to `/` from history, bookmarks, or tab restore, so the phone reopens straight into the app instead of a 401 dead end (see Security model). - **PC side**: the same link opens the full desktop Web GUI on another computer over the gated `/remote` channel; unpaired PCs see a guided blocking page (with a manual pair-token input) and no workspace data behind it. - **Security**: one active token at a time (a refresh invalidates the old link; the link stays re-usable within its expiry window so a scan handed between browsers can complete pairing; it expires). 停止 revokes every paired device and the current token — the `/remote` channel cuts them off on their next request. Pairing is this plugin's access control for the `/remote` channel; direct `/api` on a LAN-exposed bind is governed by the harness fence + browser auth (see Security model). Loopback (127.0.0.1) keeps using `/api` directly, and so does a page an application on this machine delivered — the desktop shell's `dsh-app://app/` or a `file:` page — because a pairing link is reachable only over the network. A paired device is a **full-control credential** (see Security model). - **LAN bind toggle**: the settings card writes a managed block into the profile `cordis.patch.yml` that pins the webserver bind to `0.0.0.0` (on) or `127.0.0.1` (off) — no `--host` command-line dance; an explicit `--host`/`--port` flag still wins. It maintains the matching host firewall rule (Windows Defender via netsh; Linux firewalld/ufw/iptables; other platforms report the firewall as unmanaged) and shows the live bind, the reachable LAN URLs, and the firewall state. - **Live status**: the desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; an `/api` posture probe reports any host whose `/api` fence the SDK leaves open, and the auto-tunnel state appears on the panel while the tunnel is starting. - **Self-update lives next door**: the one-click family update is its own plugin (`dsh-update`, the same sidebar foot seat), so turning remote access off — or disabling this plugin — never removes the update trigger. - **Desktop foot row**: on the wide sidebar the footer-action occupants share the official Settings trigger's line instead of stacking above it, so no single control owns a full-width row; any other foot block (the usage glance card, another plugin's) keeps a full row above them, and the 56px rail keeps the shell's stacked foot. ## The mobile adaptation layer The official desktop layout already auto-collapses the sidebar below 1024px. On top of that, while the viewport is portrait + coarse pointer + narrower than 1100px the plugin injects: - a CSS sheet keyed on CSS-Modules **semantic suffixes** (`[class$="_composerSeat"]`) so the selectors survive official rebuilds that only change hashes: 44px touch targets on the collapsed rail, 16px inputs (prevents iOS focus zoom), safe-area padding for the composer, compact type for the message list and sidebar, a column layout for the settings modal, and a full-width PlanReview card; - a **draggable whale button** as the entry to the collapsed sidebar (position persisted; wired to the official `ctx.layout.toggleSidebar()`), hidden while the sidebar is expanded; - **gestures**: left-swipe collapses the sidebar, right-swipe in the conversation opens it; long-pressing a session row opens the same action menu as the desktop ellipsis; tapping a session row or anywhere outside the sidebar collapses it again; - **input behavior for touch**: Enter only inserts a newline (send goes through the send button), programmatic composer focus is suppressed (no spurious keyboards), and official tooltip bubbles are hidden because taps leave them stuck; - **mobile plugin scope**: while the layer is active, the right-hand details column and the desktop-oriented tool surfaces (SSH terminal, skill explorer, task board, git graph, pet, usage) are hidden - keyed on the L2 semantic roots (`data-dsh-plugin`), so ownership stays with the declaring plugin and class churn cannot resurrect them. These are render suppressions; the client bundles still load. Activation also closes the details panel through the official `ctx.layout.closeDetails()`. - a **manual opt-out**: `sessionStorage.dsh-remote-force-desktop = 1` disables the whole layer; landscape, desktop, and wide viewports are never touched. The paired remote desktop also runs in **host mode**: on this harness line the "configuration plane is local" behavior is a client-side branch on `connection.isLoopback`, and the channel boot script installs the transport hook (`__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost = true`) before any boot entry. Host mode is **server-granted**: the hook is installed only when the device-gated app landing (`/pair-app`) published the grant marker ahead of the boot patch, so a shell served to an unpaired browser — a fence-open deployment — never poses as the machine owner. Settings, credentials, agent presets, and deliverables therefore work on the phone exactly as on the desktop — every call still rides the gated `/remote` channel. Three control planes stay physically local: `/api/pair/*`, `/api/update/*`, and `/api/plugin-manager/*`. ## Requirements - A DSH installation whose `dsh` CLI supports profiles (`dsh --profile`, `dsh plugin`) — the profile/bundle mechanism this package rides on. - For LAN use, either flip the **局域网访问** toggle in the settings card (writes the bind block; effective from the next `dsh web` start) or start with `dsh web --host 0.0.0.0`. With the default `127.0.0.1` bind the panel shows an explicit explanation instead of a dead QR code — unless a public base URL is configured (see "Remote access over the internet" below), which makes the QR reachable from anywhere without rebinding. The panel's mint/stop endpoints are loopback-only by design: a desktop browser opened at the LAN URL sees a "配对面板仅限本机使用" banner. - For the one-click public tunnel (`autoTunnel`), the `cloudflared` platform binary ships with the package (its postinstall downloads it; a runtime download covers installers that skip postinstall scripts). No user-side tooling, account, or domain is needed. - The same binary also powers the fixed-hostname named-tunnel mode (`tunnelToken`): the public hostname never changes, so a paired phone keeps its bookmark and its pairing cookie across restarts and never re-pairs. ## Install Install the family aggregate package `@linxin666/dsh-web-all` (all plugins and skins in one) or this plugin alone: ```sh # Recommended: install directly from npm dsh plugin --profile web add @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui@latest # Or from the repository (development loop) git clone https://github.com/zhu1090093659/dsh-web.git cd dsh-web pnpm install && pnpm -r build dsh plugin --profile web add link:$(pwd)/packages/dsh-remote-web-ui ``` Restart the profile (`dsh web`), then open the phone icon in the sidebar foot. The plugin's `cordis.patch.yml` inserts the single plugin row that mounts both halves. > `github:/` installs work for a standalone repo whose package sits at the root (the `prepare` script builds `lib/` during install; pnpm ≥10 blocks that until you copy the printed key into the profile's `pnpm-workspace.yaml` `allowBuilds` and re-run). Monorepo subpackages use the `link:` form above. ## Use 1. Open the settings card (设置 → Web 插件 → 远程访问) and flip **局域网访问** on if the server binds loopback; the card shows the live bind, the firewall state, and the reachable LAN URLs. The bind change takes effect from the next `dsh web` start. 2. Start `dsh web`, click the phone icon, and the panel mints a fresh time-limited QR. 3. Scan with the phone (or open the copied link): the device pairs and boots the **official Web GUI** served cookieless by the plugin (`/pair-accept` → `/pair-app`), which reloads into `/`. On a phone, the portrait adaptation layer is already active — same layout as the desktop, same live state. Later reopens from history or a bookmark go straight back into the app (https origins; see Security model). 4. **To pair a PC instead**: copy the same link and open it in a browser on the other computer. After the same round trip the full Web GUI runs there over the gated `/remote` channel; unpaired PCs see the guided blocking page and no data. One active token pairs one device; mint a fresh QR for the next device. 5. The desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; the device roster lists the paired devices with per-device 取消配对, and 停止 revokes everything. 6. Configure pairing lifetime, device limits, the LAN fence policy (`requirePairingForLan`), the public base URL, the auto tunnel, the stable-hostname relay, and the named-tunnel token in the same settings card. ## Remote access over the internet (tunnels) A tunnel process restart — most often a mobile network dropping and reconnecting — used to drop the public host from the pairing fence the moment the tunnel left `running`, so the address still printed in the QR code answered 403, including on the deliberately public `/api/pair/status` (issue #1547). A named tunnel's fixed hostname and a registered relay origin never change, so both now stay trusted throughout the reconnect; a quick tunnel's previous host stays trusted for a 60 s grace window, because the edge may still be delivering a connection the phone already opened, and is dropped only if the tunnel has not come back by then. ### One-click public tunnel (recommended) Set **自动公网隧道** (autoTunnel) in the settings card. The plugin runs its own Cloudflare quick tunnel (`cloudflared` ships with the package), feeds the minted public URL into the QR base and the pairing fence dynamically, and keeps the posture probe informed — a phone anywhere can pair at any time. The manual public address and the named-tunnel token below are ignored while this is on. The minted hostname is ephemeral and changes on every `dsh web` restart — the stable-hostname relay below keeps the phone's origin fixed across those restarts. ### Stable-hostname relay (default on; pair once across restarts) While the quick tunnel runs, the plugin additionally registers its current tunnel URL with the dsh-market relay registry and rebuilds the QR on a fixed origin — `https://.dsh-market.com` — minted once per profile and stored under `$DSH_HOME/remote-web-ui-registry/`. The hostname never changes, so the phone's bookmark and its pairing cookie keep working across `dsh web` restarts with no Cloudflare account, no dashboard, and no domain of your own. - Registration is secret-authenticated: the plugin mints a 256-bit secret next to the identity and re-syncs the mapping on every tunnel start (crash restarts included) with capped backoff. If the registry is unreachable, the QR falls back to the raw quick URL for that session and the panel says so. - A phone opening the stable origin while the instance is offline sees an explicit "instance offline — refresh in a moment, no re-pairing needed" page instead of a dead link. - Turn **固定域名中继** (relay) off in the settings card to keep the deployment entirely on the ephemeral origin; the registry row is removed at once. Trust note: relayed traffic transits the dsh-market edge (a Cloudflare Worker operated by the package author) — see Security model. ### Fixed-hostname named tunnel (bring your own domain) The relay above already fixes the phone's origin on a shared dsh-market subdomain. A Cloudflare named tunnel is the alternative for deployments that want a hostname on **their own** domain: its public hostname is permanent, so the phone's bookmark and its pairing cookie keep working across `dsh web` restarts — pair once, never again (until the session idles past `idleExpireMs`). 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard create a Tunnel and map a public hostname — e.g. `dsh.example.com` — to `http://127.0.0.1:3080` (the port `dsh web` listens on). 2. Copy the tunnel's token and paste it into **固定域名隧道令牌** (tunnelToken) in the settings card. 3. Set the same hostname as **公网地址** (publicBaseUrl). The token does not carry the hostname, so without this step the tunnel stays off and a warning names the missing piece. The plugin then runs `cloudflared tunnel run --token` with the same lifecycle management as the quick tunnel: the binary ships with the package, unexpected exits restart with backoff, a running tunnel's public URL is probed every 60 s and two consecutive failures mint a fresh tunnel through that same restart path, and the posture probe audits the `/api` fence for the fixed host. The token is stored as a settings secret and read back redacted. The auto quick tunnel takes precedence while it is on. A `running` tunnel is not a terminal state: a connector that lost its Cloudflare edge registration keeps its process and its metrics port alive while the minted hostname stops resolving, so the plugin used to report `running` indefinitely and the relay kept forwarding the phone to the dead address (Cloudflare 530 / Error 1016) instead of the relay's offline page (issue #1723). The readiness watchdog now treats a public URL that stops answering — DNS failure, refused connection, or a Cloudflare 5xx such as 530 — as a dead tunnel after two consecutive probes, and the ordinary backoff restart mints a new URL and re-registers the relay. An unauthenticated `401`/`403` answer still counts as alive, because that is a healthy round trip to a harness that has not been paired yet. ### Manual tunnels (bring your own) Expose the local port with any tunnel and set **公网地址** (publicBaseUrl), e.g.: ```sh # 1. Expose the local port (whatever dsh web is listening on): cloudflared tunnel --url http://127.0.0.1:3080 # prints something like: https://xxxx-xxxx-xxxx.trycloudflare.com # 2. Start dsh web as usual. Do not add --trusted-host for the tunnel # domain unless you intentionally want the SDK to trust that host for # /api. Keep the LAN bind off if only tunnel access is wanted. ``` Then set the printed URL as 公网地址. The QR link is built from it, and the plugin's pairing fence accepts the tunneled authority. The posture probe keeps auditing which `/api` authorities the SDK fence leaves open. ## Development Work from this repository (no sibling checkout needed): ```sh cd dsh-web export NPM_TOKEN='' # only if private @deepseek-ai auth is still required pnpm install pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui run build pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui test pnpm --filter @linxin666/dsh-remote-web-ui run typecheck ``` The peer APIs come from the official NPM SDK: every `@deepseek-ai/*` package used here is declared in devDependencies (0.2.0-rc.2 cohort), and TypeScript/Vitest resolve types straight from node_modules — no DSH source checkout is required. The consumer-side `prepare` build (`tsdown.prepare.config.ts`) transpiles without type checking, so git installs work without any harness checkout either. ## Checks ```sh pnpm run typecheck pnpm test pnpm run build ``` ## Harness contract dependencies Pinned to the 0.2.0-rc.2 line; the seams this build relies on: - **`sidebar.footer.action` foot seat** (the 0.1.7 shell composition): the sidebar declares and renders the seat the remote entry occupies. - **`ctx.layout.toggleSidebar()`** (packages/client/ui-layout): the whale button expands the collapsed sidebar through the official panel-action face. - **`ctx.connection.authenticatedUrl()`** (packages/client/connection): the sanctioned launch-token seam the proxy redeems once for its inner credential (`src/inner-auth.ts`), so re-issued `/api` calls satisfy the harness browser-auth check. - **`__DSH_FILE_UPLOAD__`** (file-upload client hooks): the optional pre-Cordis transport the upload service reads once at construction. The remote boot patch publishes it so background uploads stay on the rewritten main-thread fetch instead of a Web Worker that escapes the channel (issue #1580). - **`__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost`** (client-connection transport hooks): the host-mode flip for paired remote desktops. It is installed only when the device-gated app landing published the `__DSH_REMOTE_HOST_GRANT__` marker ahead of the boot patch, so the flip is server-granted rather than asserted from the origin. There is no host-side per-method privilege pin on this line — the configuration plane branches on `connection.isLoopback` in the client — and no `api/gate` waterfall either (the gate listener stays mounted for deployments that gain the seam; pairing enforcement lives on this plugin's own `/remote` channel). - **User-patch bind semantics**: same-id patch rows replace the row config wholesale, and the user patch layer cannot evaluate `webStartup`-dependent `!!js` expressions reliably — the LAN bind block therefore materializes static values and the plugin re-asserts it every boot. The fence helpers (`isTrustedApiRequest` / `isLoopbackHostname`) are reimplemented locally in `src/gate.ts` / `src/routes.ts`: the connection plugin stopped exporting them, so the pairing routes carry their own copy scoped to the literals the QR links advertise. ## Manual E2E: LAN pairing round trip The unit/component specs cover the route family, the gate, the channel, the lan-bind block, and the adaptation layer, but the pairing loop involves a real browser on a non-loopback origin. Repeat this after any change to the wire contract or the connection loop: 1. Start an isolated instance: `DSH_HOME=/tmp/dsh-qa dsh --profile web --no-open --port 3191` with the LAN bind toggle on (or a profile whose bind block pins 0.0.0.0). 2. Open the **loopback** URL (`http://127.0.0.1:3191`) in a browser: the phone icon sits in the sidebar foot; the panel mints a QR whose link is `/pair-accept?pair=`. 3. In a second tab under mobile emulation (390x844, touch) open that link: the chain `/pair-accept → /pair-app?grant= → /` sets the device cookie, spends the grant, serves the patched official shell, and boots the UI — `document.body.classList` carries `dsh-remote-portrait`, the adaptation stylesheet and the whale button exist, and `__DSH_TRANSPORT__.ownsHost` is `true`. The settings surface renders host data (host mode), not a memory mirror. In an https deployment the shell also registers the reopen service worker (`/pair-app.sw.js`); reloading `/` in that tab boots the app instead of the harness 401. 4. The desktop badge flips to 已连接 in real time; a LAN-origin desktop page instead shows the 配对面板仅限本机使用 banner and opens no status stream. 5. 停止 on the desktop cuts the device off: its next request 403s with `unpaired` (the fence page offers the manual pair-token input). The public path is the same round trip through a tunnel (see "Remote access over the internet"): loopback mint → device opens the public QR URL → accept → official UI. Only `publicBaseUrl` (plugin config) names the tunneled host; `--trusted-host` is not part of this pairing flow. The desktop panel still opens at `http://127.0.0.1`. ## Security model - **Pairing is the access control for the `/remote` channel, unconditionally**: every request must carry a live paired-device cookie, enforced before any bytes are forwarded. A missing or revoked session receives HTTP 403 with a JSON rejection carrying `error.code: "unpaired"`; the browser's `EventSource` API exposes only the stream failure, not that response body. This gate does **not** follow `requirePairingForLan`: the channel re-issues every call with the process's own browser-auth credential, so admitting an unpaired caller would hand out that authority. The LAN policy governs the plain `/api` surface only and can never widen the channel (issue #1665). - **The channel carries the process's own inner credential.** The harness browser-auth cookie is authority-bound (minted for the exact `host:port` a browser visited) and has no loopback exemption, so a proxied re-issue to `127.0.0.1` cannot reuse a device's cookie. The plugin therefore redeems its own launch token once — the same exchange a first browser visit performs — and attaches that cookie to re-issued requests. The credential is only ever exercised behind the pairing gate above; 停止/取消配对 immediately stop exercising it. - **Runtime reality: pairing does not gate direct `/api`.** Nothing in the official runtime emits the `api/gate` seam (verified against the 0.2.0-rc.2 packages installed by this repository), so a direct `/api` call from a LAN origin is governed solely by the harness fence (which auto-trusts LAN literals under a `0.0.0.0` bind) plus the harness browser-auth cookie. A browser credential a device has already redeemed therefore survives 停止/取消配对 until its natural expiry (30 days) — revocation binds the `/remote` channel and the pairing cookie, not that credential. The plugin probes the `/api` posture and warns loudly; treat a LAN-exposed bind as a deliberate decision, and prefer loopback plus tunnels when the machine is shared. - **A paired device is a full-control credential.** With host mode active it reaches the complete host API — chat, sessions, settings, credentials, agent presets, deliverables — mirroring the SDK's own stance that a loopback desktop is trusted. Only the three control planes (pairing, self-update, plugin install/remove) stay physically local. Only pair devices you control; 停止 or per-device 取消配对 revokes immediately. - **Control endpoints stay loopback-only**: mint/stop/revoke, the device roster, and the lan-bind status answer only to loopback, and the gated channel keeps the self-update and plugin-install paths physically local. A LAN-origin browser sees the "配对面板仅限本机使用" banner. - **Background file uploads ride the channel too.** The official upload service prefers a Web Worker carrier whose own globals no main-thread patch reaches, so the boot patch (and the browser patch as a fallback) publishes the official pre-Cordis hook `__DSH_FILE_UPLOAD__` and hands it the patched `fetch`: the raw `/api/session/uploadFileBinary` POST is rewritten onto `/remote` and carries the device credential exactly like every other gated call. Without the hook a paired browser's uploads bypass the channel and the harness browser-auth fence answers 401 (issue #1580). # deepseek-harness-plugins

Unofficial plugins, local forks, presets, skills, and maintenance tools for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). This is a source collection, not a single installable plugin or a distribution of DSH.

## Contents

- [Compatibility](#compatibility)
- [Plugins and presets](#plugins-and-presets)
- [Skills](#skills)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Development](#development)
- [Repository scope and ownership](#repository-scope-and-ownership)
- [License](#license)

## Compatibility

Choose an individual package and read its README before installing it. Packages target different DSH releases; presence in this repository does not mean a package supports your installed version.

- [DSH Evolve](dsh-evolve/README.md) declares DSH `0.2.1-rc.3` and Node.js `>=24.9.0`.
- [Prompt Compact](dsh-prompt-compact/README.md) targets DSH `0.2.1` and only replaces upstream prompt text whose fingerprint matches its reviewed version.
- The root [pnpm workspace](pnpm-workspace.yaml) retains development dependencies from the DSH `0.1.0-rc.8` line. Its build and test scripts are not a repository-wide compatibility check.
- [Compatibility copies](compat/) and older adapters have package-specific requirements. In particular, the Web Search and Cursor invariant companions depend on a registry absent from current DSH master. Do not treat their older installation examples as current-version guidance.

The [maintenance scope](docs/maintenance-scope.md) distinguishes maintained extensions, retained reference implementations, and removed managed providers. The `managed-standard` and `managed-cordis` preset names do not imply use of those removed providers.

## Plugins and presets

These entry points describe each component's setup, behavior, and limitations; this is not an install-all list.

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [DSH Evolve](dsh-evolve/README.md) | Observes tool failures and repeated calls. Installation defaults to observation without LLM calls; proposal generation is opt-in, and activation and rollback require human commands. |
| [Prompt Compact](dsh-prompt-compact/README.md) | Opt-in, preset-scoped alternatives for the Workflow and Ralph prompt sections. Tool schemas and execution behavior remain unchanged; it registers no Cordis Skill. |
| [Goal acceptance](dsh-goal-acceptance/README.md) | Retains the original request and checks evidence records for Goal completion and initial delegation. See the [restricted pilot](dsh-request-acceptance-pilot/README.md) before enabling it in a shared Host. |
| [Workflow result selection](dsh-workflow-results/README.md) | Saves a complete workflow result before returning selected fields through `resultKeys`; requires a tool replacement in the chosen preset. |
| [Codex transport recovery](dsh-codex-transport-recovery/README.md) | Classifies specific premature WebSocket closures as transport errors so the official retry policy can handle them. Does not add retries or change models. |
| [AI reference-store daily preset](presets/ai-reference-store-daily/README.md) | Declares the preset for a separately configured reference-store application. Selecting the preset does not start a daily batch. |

Older integrations and local forks:

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| [Web Search](dsh-web-search/README.md) — `@kkiyama117/dsh-web-search` | Keyless DuckDuckGo HTML search, ported from [pi-web-access](https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-web-access). |
| [Cursor adapter](dsh-llm-cursor/README.md) — `@kkiyama117/dsh-llm-cursor` | Runs a Cursor SDK agent for each harness model call, with replay-state session continuity. |
| [Web UI family](dsh-web-ui/packages/) | Local copies of UI, SSH, Git graph, settings, and Modlens packages; consult each package's README. |
| [Market](dsh-market/README.md) | Local plugin-market copy with its own build and compatibility checks. |

Additional package sources live at the repository root; profile declarations live under [presets/](presets/). Neither directory is a deployment inventory.

## Skills

[skills/](skills/) contains authored skills and upstream-derived copies. Cloning this repository does not install or enable them. Local deployments may link individual skill directories into a DSH skill search path; edit the source directory, not a separate copied version. Read each skill's prerequisites before enabling it.

| Skill | Purpose and prerequisites |
|---|---|
| [issue-driven-development](skills/issue-driven-development/SKILL.md) | Shared issue intake, feature and bugfix delivery, verification, and development-process improvement for humans and AI agents. See [contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) for this repository's setup. |
| [orchestrate-agents](skills/orchestrate-agents/SKILL.md) | Task formulation, direct-versus-delegated execution, and bounded orchestration. See its [runtime limits](skills/orchestrate-agents/README.md). |
| [archify](skills/archify/SKILL.md) | Local fork of [archify](https://github.com/tt-a1i/archify) for architecture visualization, with screenshot checks at 1920×1080 and 2048×1320. |
| [quint-lang](skills/quint-lang/SKILL.md) | Quint syntax and CLI reference, imported from [quint-llm-kit](https://github.com/quint-co/quint-llm-kit). |
| [quint-modeling](skills/quint-modeling/SKILL.md) | Build or review Quint specifications from requirements or source code. |
| [quint-execute-spec](skills/quint-execute-spec/SKILL.md) | Implement code against an existing Quint specification. |
| [quint-cli](skills/quint-cli/SKILL.md) | Container-based Quint CLI instructions; requires the documented container tool and image. |
| [quint-verify](skills/quint-verify/SKILL.md) | Run invariant and witness checks and produce a structured verification report. Requires the documented Quint container environment. |
| [slack-reference-intake](skills/slack-reference-intake/SKILL.md) | Reference intake for a separately configured private Go aistore, with authorized Slack access and DSH credentials. Not a standalone public demo. |
| [implement-task](skills/implement-task/SKILL.md) | Retained implementation-flow reference with a [Quint specification](skills/implement-task/spec/README.md). It depends on legacy `subagent-fallback` tools; migrate the callers and specification before using it with current DSH. |

## Installation

1. Install DSH separately and choose the target profile.
2. Check the selected package's README, manifest, and patch for DSH compatibility, prerequisites, and activation scope. Build compiled packages using their own development instructions before loading them.
3. Install only the selected bundle through DSH's Plugin Manager or plugin CLI. A bundle declares `dsh.bundle.patch` in its package manifest; the repository root and plain skill directories are not bundles.
4. Complete any package-specific opt-in steps. For example, Prompt Compact has an empty bundle patch and needs a row in a locally authored preset. DSH Evolve instead mounts in observation mode on installation.

For CLI usage from a DSH source checkout:

```sh
pnpm dsh plugin --help
```

Use your own package location rather than the maintainer's filesystem paths in older examples. See the upstream [bundle publishing guide](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/blob/master/docs/user/develop/basic/publish.md) for profile installation. Do not edit shipped DSH presets to enable these extensions.

## Development

Use [Issues](https://github.com/kkiyama117/deepseek-harness-plugins/issues) to report problems or propose improvements. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) describes the shared human/AI development flow and this repository's verification and publication scope.

The root [package manifest](package.json) pins pnpm to `11.7.0`. The root workspace includes Web Search, Cursor, and five Web UI family packages—not every package in this repository.

| Root command | Scope |
|---|---|
| `pnpm install` | Installs dependencies for the root workspace using its lockfile. |
| `pnpm build` | Runs the build script of each workspace member. Builds are not all plain `tsc`; UI packages also bundle client assets. |
| `pnpm test` | Runs workspace-member test scripts with workspace concurrency set to one. |

For packages outside that workspace, follow their own README and package scripts. Do not use a passing root build or test run as evidence that those packages work with your DSH version. Compiled packages load generated output, not edited source; follow the package's rebuild and reload instructions.

The read-only [local setup diagnostic](scripts/local-setup.mjs) inspects a local DSH profile. It imports `dsh-market/lib/check.js`, so it requires a built Market package, which is outside the root workspace. It is not a fresh-clone setup command or an installer.

## Repository scope and ownership

This repository publishes plugin, preset, skill, test, and maintenance-tool sources. Credentials, private design and review material, execution reports, deployment inventories, local caches, and release archives stay outside Git. Review new files for sensitive data before committing; ignore rules are not a secret scanner.

The public history starts with a source-only snapshot; earlier local history is not available here. See [architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md) for composition and verification limits, and the [source ownership policy](SOURCE-OWNERSHIP.md) for the upstream Core baseline and reviewed exception.

## License

[MIT](LICENSE). Preserve the upstream license and attribution notices included with imported code, forks, and skills.

# @kkiyama117/dsh-slack-intake

## Summary

This package provides two separate DSH entries for the Go `aistore` CLI. The bundle patch mounts a standalone command adapter with local `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` credential access. The `./agent` entry registers `aistore_native_task` in an Agent scope and runs one claimed reader or reviewer task through an explicitly selected native subagent provider. Both entries require absolute paths to the `aistore` executable and store; legacy Python and `skillRoot` configuration is rejected.

## Table of Contents

- [Use the standalone adapter](#use-the-standalone-adapter)
- [Mount the native Agent entry](#mount-the-native-agent-entry)
- [Security and lifecycle](#security-and-lifecycle)
- [Verification](#verification)
- [Known limitations](#known-limitations)

-----

## Use the standalone adapter

The package declares `cordis.patch.yml` as its DSH bundle patch. The patch inserts `@deepseek-ai/dsh-credentials-local` and the standalone package entry. Set both non-secret variables to trusted absolute paths before launching the profile:

```sh
export DSH_AISTORE_EXECUTABLE=/absolute/path/aistore
export DSH_AISTORE_STORE_ROOT=/absolute/path/store
```

The deployment owner may instead override the two fields in a later profile patch:

```yaml
- id: aistore-adapter
  config:
    aistoreExecutable: /absolute/path/aistore
    storeRoot: /absolute/path/store
```

The standalone entry accepts these adapter-owned credential commands:

```sh
dsh --profile <standalone-profile> credential status
dsh --profile <standalone-profile> credential import --file /absolute/private/key
```

Every other argument sequence is passed after the fixed global arguments `--store STORE --json`. These examples match the current Go grammar:

```sh
dsh --profile <standalone-profile> verify
dsh --profile <standalone-profile> intake resume --run run:20260923-01
dsh --profile <standalone-profile> intake resume --run run:20260923-01 --allow-network
```

Only the exact `intake resume ... --allow-network` operation resolves `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. Exit code `0` means completion, and exit code `3` preserves a Go handoff. Other exits become fixed adapter diagnostics. This package does not expose a package binary; profile installation and activation remain deployment-owner operations and were not run during offline verification.

-----

## Mount the native Agent entry

Mount `@kkiyama117/dsh-slack-intake/agent` in an authored Agent preset that already consumes the host `tools`, `subagents`, and `sessionQuery` services. Do not mount it in the standalone authentication profile: that profile has no calling Agent. A preset row has this configuration:

```yaml
- id: aistore-native-task
  name: '@kkiyama117/dsh-slack-intake/agent'
  config:
    aistoreExecutable: /absolute/path/aistore
    storeRoot: /absolute/path/store
    subagentProvider: spawn
```

The configured provider must support `agentOptions`, `outputSchema`, and `agentPreset`; the in-process `spawn` provider supports all three. Install `@local/dsh-aistore-native-preset` in every calling profile. The adapter selects its `aistore-native` preset, which excludes global tools and provides no task tools; the runtime adds only `structured_output`. A missing preset rejects creation instead of inheriting parent tools. The tool must be invoked by the DSH Agent loop so `exec.agent` identifies the real parent Agent.

The tool accepts only `taskId` and `inputHash` from an aistore handoff. It performs this sequence once:

1. `task claim --id TASK --input HASH`
2. save the private claim in an owner-only temporary file
3. `task in-flight --receipt CLAIM`
4. `intake native packet --task TASK`
5. run one native child with the packet's fixed provider, model, reasoning effort, token limit, and deadline
6. verify the recorded request route, model source, session, completed turn, and exact structured-output bytes
7. `intake native accept --task TASK --attempt N --receipt RECEIPT`

A Reader result must contain each packet identity exactly once. Its status is either `ready`, with stored-source references and verbatim anchors, or `insufficient`, with a reason. The adapter validates this structured output before receipt creation; it does not translate unknown statuses such as `verified`.

A failure after the in-flight transition calls bounded `task unknown` once. The adapter does not claim or execute the task again, and it never selects another model or provider.

-----

## Security and lifecycle

The standalone subprocess receives a new environment containing only `LANG=C.UTF-8` and the credential needed for its operation: `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` for `intake slack collect`, or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` for an allowed network resume. The value is absent from argv, configuration, returned JSON, and diagnostics. Credential import accepts only an absolute owner-only regular file in an owner-only real parent directory and verifies the stored value without printing it.

Every aistore subprocess uses an argv array with no shell, ignored stdin, an 8,000,000-byte stdout limit, and a 1,024-byte stderr inspection limit. For Slack collection failures, only an exact allowlisted condition becomes an `AISTORE_SLACK_*` diagnostic; raw stderr, unknown conditions, oversized diagnostics and credential-bearing text are never exposed. Successful output must be one protocol-version-1 JSON envelope. The native claim and authority data stay outside the child prompt and tool output. Only the Go-produced native packet becomes model-visible.

The native entry uses `startActivation` with caller delivery, enforces the packet deadline, and awaits the result and `dispose()` before returning. The admission signal covers startup; after publication, cancellation disposes that exact activation. It reads the settled child's durable Session through `sessionQuery.readSession`, verifies the child id, and builds its receipt from recorded request and assistant events rather than a model's route claim. `reported_cost` is `null` because the current DSH session events do not expose a monetary cost for this run.

-----

## Verification

Run the package's offline suite against the built host named explicitly by `DSH_HOST_ROOT`. Supplying both Go binaries also enables the disposable-store integration smoke:

```sh
out=$(mktemp -d)
CGO_ENABLED=0 go -C /absolute/path/to/ai-store-go build -trimpath -o "$out/aistore" ./cmd/aistore
CGO_ENABLED=0 go -C /absolute/path/to/ai-store-go build -trimpath -o "$out/aistore-test-fixture" ./cmd/aistore-test-fixture
DSH_HOST_ROOT=/data/softwares/deepseek-harness-master \
  AISTORE_BINARY="$out/aistore" \
  AISTORE_FIXTURE_BINARY="$out/aistore-test-fixture" \
  npm test
```

The suite uses synthetic credentials and temporary files only. It starts real local child processes, preserves exit-code-3 handoffs, exercises the current built DSH tool registry, creates a real parent Agent as `exec.agent`, starts a real in-process managed activation through `spawn`, and uses a scripted local LLM adapter to produce structured output. With the two binary variables set, it creates a schema-7 disposable store and drives real Go claim, in-flight, packet, native accept, deadline, cancellation, and unknown-task rejection paths. It does not contact Slack, OpenRouter, or another network service.

-----

## Daily application

The `./daily` Host entry runs a deterministic driver over the existing Go/native entries. Launch it through an installed profile with the base Host registries, one explicitly selected minimal preset, pinned model routes, and the standalone adapter rows disabled. It exposes `daily run`, read-only `daily status`, and `daily check` (mount validation and a disposable real parent Session, with zero model turns). DSH 0.2.1 profiles use `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset-registry` and a bundle-carried `@deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-preset` declaration; the daily entry resolves the preset and rejects its activation diagnostic before claiming work.

On Linux, `daily-start.sh WAIT_SECONDS MOUNT STORE NODE CLI [CLI_ARGS...]` waits for the mount, store directory, executable Node, and readable official CLI before changing directory and executing the CLI. Install this launcher on an already available filesystem and set the systemd service's initial working directory there; an unavailable `WorkingDirectory` fails before an `ExecStartPre` can wait. Readiness expiry exits 75 without starting intake. The service's overall timeout also bounds this wait.

The driver freezes a Slack window and resumes unfinished batches before creating another. Go commits the export association and collection checkpoint together, fixes one run ID, and enforces campaign-wide native/classifier budgets inside the claim transaction. The driver holds a separate Go-backed filesystem lock until all children and reporting work have stopped. Losing the driver closes the lock child's stdin; cancellation alone does not release ownership early.

Reader articles receive a fresh-context `content_review` task, with the article hashes and the Reader's saved public source bodies. The review must cover every article exactly once with `approve`, `reject`, or `insufficient` and a concrete reason. Only accepted approvals reach Jev; quote matching is not a semantic approval. A second call to the same model can share its errors and is not proof of factual correctness.

Configure all deployment paths (`aistoreExecutable`, `storeRoot`, `intakeConfig`, `reportsRoot`, `backupsRoot`, `notifyExecutable`), `presetId`, an explicit idle `parentRoute`, and positive `deadlineSeconds`, `cleanupSeconds`, `notificationSeconds`, `exitGraceSeconds`, and `maxTransitions`. The parent is never prompted; it owns the native tool calls. The daily parent allows only `aistore_native_task`; its children allow only their scoped structured-output tool. Disable title-generation and automatic LLM retries in this profile so they cannot incur unrelated calls.

Private JSON/Markdown reports preserve counts, task states, reported costs and missing-cost flags. Desktop notification failure does not restart intake. A fully processed batch can finish with terminal held items while its human-facing status remains `needs_attention`; that is not a claim that every article was registered. Reposts of already-held identities carry the hold forward without new dispatch. Pending, active and unknown attempts prevent batch completion, so a new date cannot bypass their budget. Batches with new registrations require a verified backup before final completion; an incomplete backup is retained and needs operator attention. Over-limit exports remain attached to the unfinished batch. The daily cap applies to native task attempts, not a guaranteed monetary total.

After the parent and native workers have settled, the daily entry requests the official launcher's application disposal. An unreferenced `exitGraceSeconds` timer bounds any residual process handles: it preserves the requested exit code only when the launcher has recorded completion of its application disposer; otherwise it exits with failure. A grace expiry records resource types and the disposal observation in the journal. This does not claim that the underlying provider's handle leak is repaired, and the systemd process-group timeout remains the outer limit.

Reviewer output accepts only `classified` with an existing taxonomy key, or `needs_review`/`excluded` with a null category, and requires a reason. Unsupported statuses are not translated. A malformed result accepted by an older adapter is retained as evidence and reported as a terminal hold rather than published or retried.

The native entry accepts an optional absolute `receiptRoot`. After a dispatched task fails or acceptance becomes uncertain, it retains the private temporary directory there (or in the OS temporary directory for older configurations). Do not delete these receipts before reconciliation. Unknown attempts are never automatically replayed. A failed daily batch stops without switching models, issuing grants, or modifying the taxonomy.

## Slack daily-report bridge (2026-10-06)

The separately mounted `./bridge` Host entry reuses Go collection/classification records, posts completed-batch digests, receives authorized seven-policy selections over Socket Mode, and runs one durable development-verification job at a time. It does not change the original standalone, Reader/Reviewer, or daily driver entries. The installable local bundle and operator guide are [here](/data/softwares/slack-intake/docs/slack-digest-automation-2026-10-06.md).

The bridge requires a pinned team/channel, explicit human-user allowlist, a bot credential with posting/channel-info scopes, and an app-level Socket Mode credential from the same Slack App. Normalized decisions reach a private durable inbox before ACK; Go owns policy versions, atomic outbox, separate SQLite jobs and replay guards. Notification retries never re-run verification. Unknown job and message-send outcomes are retained for reconciliation.

The verification Session supplies only `development_read`, `development_command`, and `verification_result` in native mode. Its project cwd, route, deadline and steps are configured; cwd is not an OS filesystem sandbox. A successful command is necessary for a model-reported verified result, but semantic correctness is not independently certified. Costs remain unknown unless separately observed.
