## Install

```powershell
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-archive-favorites-forge
```

Then **fully quit and reopen DSH**. The host half (`lib/index.js`) has no
watcher in this harness generation, and the client bundle is snapshotted at
startup — so a page refresh alone does **not** pick up a new version.

## How it works

```
lib/index.js    host half   — favourites store, transcript-path resolver,
                              JSON routes, guarded delete, archive/dearchive,
                              file snapshots + transcript-log parsing
lib/client.js   client half — official slot registrations + two DOM rules
                              (the favourites filter and the transcript buttons)
```

**Slots used** (all documented in the harness client contract):

| Slot | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| `sidebar.workspaces.session.menu.item` | 4 rows: favourite, copy id+path, continue in a new window, delete |
| `sidebar.workspaces.session.row.action` | 1 hover ☆ star |
| `settings.section` | the 归档收藏 page |
| `shell.overlay` | the one confirmation modal used by edit-resend and undo |

**Host routes** (all under `/plugins/dsh-archive-favorites-forge`):

| Route | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `GET /status` | version + state paths, for diagnostics |
| `GET /favorites`, `POST /favorite` | the favourites set |
| `GET /archived`, `POST /unarchive` | the archived set, and undo of one archive |
| `GET\|POST /idle-archive` | preview and apply the idle batch archive |
| `POST /export-list` | write the tab-separated list |
| `POST /reveal` | open the file manager on a path |
| `POST /session-info` | one session's title / workspace / transcript path |
| `POST /delete` | guarded permanent delete (batch) |
| `POST /session-turn-info` | one turn's user text, its file-change list, and the fork boundary |
| `POST /session-files-restore` | roll back the files changed after a given sequence number |
| `POST /session-replace` | retire the original conversation after a fork took its place |
| `POST /session-digest` | read-only: distil a long conversation into a requirement-timeline + task-progress brief for a fresh window |
| `POST /ungrouped-diagnose` | read-only health check: which conversations would land in "Ungrouped", why, and what to do |
| `POST /ungrouped-cleanup` | one-click cleanup; **dry run unless `confirm: true`**, and it re-diagnoses before acting |
| `POST /ungrouped-explain` | the prose answer to "why does Ungrouped exist, and is it from deleting conversations?" |
| `GET\|POST /ghost-cache-diagnose` | read-only: orphan projection-cache records whose session directory is gone |
| `POST /ghost-cache-clean` | recycle orphan cache files; **dry run unless `confirm: true`**, re-scans first, pinned records kept by default |

Every contribution is registered through `ctx.slots.inject` — the "register once
the owning entry is mounted" contract — so the plugin never assumes the sidebar
is up, and never holds a reference to a node the host owns.

Two DOM rules exist, both deliberate exceptions:

- **The favourites filter.** The view-options menu is a plain array with **no
  slot and no trigger id**, so that single control is added by finding the
  official filter row in the DOM and cloning it.
- **The transcript buttons.** The conversation transcript has no slot for
  per-message actions either, so ↺ ✏️ 🗑 are appended after the official copy
  button under each user message. The anchor is the single `[data-clock="start"]`
  node per message, and the owner is its
  `[data-chat-flow-kind="user"][data-chat-turn]` **or**
  `[data-chat-flow-kind="steering"][data-chat-turn]` ancestor — the harness
  labels a turn-opening question `user` and a mid-turn interjection `steering`,
  and both share the same `UserMessageNodeView`, so matching `user` alone leaves
  every interjected message without buttons (fixed in 0.28.2). Never a
  CSS-module hash (those are re-hashed on every build).
  A `MutationObserver` re-runs the scan, so messages that stream in later get
  their buttons too.

### Why the favourites set lives in a file, not `localStorage`

Renderer `localStorage` is origin-scoped: the desktop shell, a phone view and a
remote browser are different origins and would each keep their own stars. The
host half persists them to

```
~/.dsh/data/dsh-archive-favorites-forge/favorites.json
```

which survives a profile switch, a reinstall, and both ends.

### Why the delete is host-side and guarded

There is **no official session-delete RPC** in this harness generation — the
shipped UI never deletes a session. "Delete this conversation" therefore means
removing the session's own artifact directory under `~/.dsh/sessions/`. That is
irreversible, so the host applies these guards before it removes anything:

1. a **favourited** id is refused outright (checked host-side, not just in the UI);
2. a resolved path **outside the sessions root** is refused;
3. a **symlink** is refused;
4. the sessions root itself is refused;
5. the batch is capped by `maxDeletePerCall`.

Each id is reported separately, so one failure never aborts the batch. After a
successful delete the host emits `api-session/removed` — the harness's own
row-removal event — so the sidebar drops the row immediately instead of showing
it until the next reload.

### Why edit and undo are "fork, then retire the original"

There is no in-place "truncate this conversation" RPC either. The only official
way to keep a prefix of a conversation is `sessions.fork({ sessionId, atSeq })`,
which produces a **new** child conversation holding everything before `atSeq`.

So both buttons do the same three-step dance:

1. **Fork** the conversation at the boundary (for the first turn there is no
   prefix to keep, so `sessions.create` opens a fresh conversation in the same
   workspace instead);
2. **Optionally roll the files back** — `POST /session-files-restore` restores
   every file the assistant touched after that boundary;
3. **Retire the original** via `POST /session-replace`, because the original is
   now superseded by its own fork and leaving it around would double every row
   in the sidebar.

Step 3 is the one place where a **favourite** conversation may be deleted, and it
is the reason `handleDelete` grew an explicit `replace` flag rather than the
client simply calling `/delete`: a favourite means "keep this conversation", and
the conversation being retired here is *the one the fork replaced*. Only the
favourite guard is skipped. Every other guard — sessions-root containment, not
the root itself, non-symlink, is-a-directory, and the EBUSY/EPERM retries — stays
on, because a fork produces an ordinary session directory and none of those
conditions have become safe. The flag is threaded as an explicit parameter on a
**separate route**, so a `/delete` request body can never switch the guard off.

`beforeSeq` (the fork boundary) is the sequence number of the event **immediately
before** the turn's `turn/start`, not the `turn/start` itself. Forking inside the
gap between `turn/start` and the first user message would leave an unclosed
`turn/start` in the child, and the fork synthesises a completed-turn line to
close it — a phantom empty turn.

### Why the file snapshots are content-addressed

Before each `write` / `edit` / `str_replace_editor` call the host copies the
file's current bytes to

```
~/.dsh/sessions/<workspace-dir>/<session-dir>/history-file/blobs/<sha256>
```

and appends one line to `history-file/manifest.jsonl`:

```json
{"seq": 412, "turn": 7, "time": "...", "tool": "edit", "path": "C:\\...", "blob": "<sha256>"}
```

`blob: null` means the file did not exist at that moment, so restoring it means
**deleting** it. Hashing the content means a file edited five times in one turn
is stored once, and rolling back consumes the manifest entries it used (and the
blobs they orphaned), so a rolled-back conversation does not keep growing.

Snapshots are written **before** the tool runs, so the very first `write` to a
brand-new file records "did not exist" rather than its post-write content.

### Why there is a log-reverse fallback

Conversations that predate this plugin have no manifest. For those, the host
re-reads the transcript (`session[.vN].jsonl.zstd`, multi-frame zstd, header line
dropped) and applies the inverse of each recorded tool call in reverse order:
`edit` swaps `new_string` back to `old_string`, `str_replace_editor create`
deletes the file, `str_replace` swaps `new_str` back to `old_str`, `insert`
removes `new_str`.

`write` cannot be inverted — a full overwrite leaves no trace of what was there —
so a conversation whose only changes came from `write` gets a **warning** naming
the file instead of a silent no-op. That warning is surfaced in the confirm
dialog, which is why the file list is fetched *before* the dialog opens.

### Why "Ungrouped" is not caused by deleting conversations

The official sidebar's `sessionVisible()` runs four checks in order:

```js
if (session.origin === "subagent") return false           // 1. subagents out
if (session.blank && session.id !== current) return false  // 2. other blanks out
case "default": return !archived.has(session.id)           // 3. archived out
// 4. only now: "is this session accounted for by a workspace?"
```

Step 3 returns `false` outright, so an archived id **never reaches** the `stray`
branch that builds the bucket. The chain "delete a conversation → its id lingers
in `archivedSessionIds` → an Ungrouped group appears" therefore does not exist in
the code. Measured counter-evidence: this machine's `archivedSessionIds` holds
**98 ids whose session directories no longer exist**, and the sidebar stayed clean
throughout.

The one real cause is: **a session was created but never accounted for by any
workspace.** If `WorkspaceRegistry.create()` misses its `attachSession`, or the
session's `cwd` points at a directory that was never registered as a workspace,
it stays stray forever. A plugin cannot intercept the official create path, so
the design is "warn once per boot" + "fix it in one click" — never a silent
auto-delete.

## Notes and limits

- **The id form**: session ids are spelled `session-<uuid>`, but artifact
  directories on an upgraded machine use **both** `<uuid>` and `session-<uuid>`.
  Every comparison goes through a normaliser and the resolver tries both
  spellings, so this works for old and new conversations alike.
- **Archived conversations cannot be opened** — that is shipped DSH behaviour,
  not this plugin's. Unarchive first if you want to read one.
- **Deleting is permanent.** It removes the conversation and its transcript. It
  does not touch your project working directory.
- **Blank sessions are never candidates.** A "blank" session is the provisional
  New Session slot; it has no content to archive and the shipped sidebar hides
  every blank session except the currently selected one, so a candidate list
  containing one would be impossible to verify. They are excluded from both the
  idle pool and the batch-delete set, and the export names the rest the way the
  sidebar does (`新会话` / `未命名`).
- **Candidate lists are intersected with what the sidebar actually lists.** A
  session that is archived but not rendered (no `cwd`) is never counted or
  acted on.
- The plugin reads the Workspace registry to map a session to its owning
  folder. It mutates that registry only through the registry's **own**
  `archiveSession` / `unarchiveSession` methods, and never writes another
  plugin's internals.
- **`新对话-<original title>` loses its last few characters when the original
  title is long.** This is a shipped DSH ceiling, not a limit this plugin adds:
  the `session-title` service sets `maxTitleBytes: 80`
  (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-base/cordis.patch.yml`) and `rename()` truncates to 80
  **UTF-8 bytes** (three bytes per CJK character, never splitting one). The
  original title `DeepSeek 智能体团队任务：蒸馏消息回滚与侧边栏未分组排查` is
  78 bytes; the 10-byte `新对话-` prefix pushes it to 88, so it is cut to 33
  characters / 79 bytes. Scanning all 574 session titles in this install, the
  longest is exactly 79 bytes — 80 is the global ceiling. The plugin passes the
  title through verbatim and imposes no length of its own; raising the limit
  means editing `session-title.config.maxTitleBytes` in the profile, which
  affects every title in the install and needs a restart.

### Limits of the file snapshots (read these before trusting a rollback)

- **Only three tools are tracked**: `write`, `edit`, and `str_replace_editor`.
  Anything else that touches a file — a shell/terminal command, a Python script
  the assistant ran, a formatter, a `git checkout` — leaves **no snapshot and no
  log record**, so undo cannot see it. If a turn edited files only through the
  terminal, undo rewinds the conversation and leaves the files alone.
- **Only absolute paths are recorded.** A relative path in a tool argument is
  skipped, because resolving it against the right base directory is not knowable
  from the transcript alone, and guessing wrong would snapshot or restore the
  wrong file.
- **A single file larger than 8 MB is skipped** (one blob per version, and the
  cap keeps one long turn from filling the disk). The skip is logged; undo will
  not restore that file.
- **Rollback overwrites whatever is there now.** It restores the pre-turn bytes,
  so edits you made by hand to the same file since then are lost. That is what
  "undo" means here, but it is worth knowing before ticking the checkbox.
- **The edit box is prefilled with the message text only.** Attachments that
  were on the original message are **not** carried over — re-attach them if the
  resend needs them. This is deliberate: attachment handles are session-scoped
  and copying one into a new conversation would produce a dangling reference.
- **Undo deletes the original conversation.** The rewind is implemented as
  fork-and-retire, so the pre-undo conversation does not survive as a hidden
  branch. Anything in it that you wanted to keep should be copied out first.
- **Blank conversations are not affected** by any of this: they have no turns
  and no tool calls.

### Limits of the Ungrouped health check

- **It treats the symptom, not the disease.** The plugin cannot intercept the
  official create path that fails to register a session, so all it can do is tell
  you which conversations are stray, why, and fix them in one click — plus warn
  once per boot.
- **Deletes always go to the recycle bin**
  (`Microsoft.VisualBasic.FileIO.FileSystem.DeleteDirectory(..., 'SendToRecycleBin')`).
  If the recycle-bin call fails it degrades to moving the directory into
  `<dshHome>/sessions_quarantine_<stamp>/`; it never hard-deletes. You clean that
  quarantine folder up yourself.
- **The conversation you are currently in is never touched automatically** — it is
  labelled "needs a human" and skipped.
- **At most 50 items per run** (`maxItems`); the rest are reported as
  `budget-exhausted` and a second click picks them up.
- **The host re-diagnoses before acting.** What the page shows is a snapshot from
  a few seconds ago, and a session may have been registered in the meantime, so
  what actually runs is "still stray right now" — not the list the client sent.
- **The check is cheap.** It decodes only the **first zstd frame** of each session
  log to read the header (the four-step exclusion test needs nothing else), and
  decodes full text only for the few sessions that actually land in the bucket.
  Measured on this machine — 653 session directories, 746 MB of logs — **0.43 s**.
  The first version decoded every frame of every log and took 12.6 s, blocking the
  main thread long enough to look like a freeze.
- **One kind of entry is invisible to the check.** Records that exist only in the
  projection cache (`~/.dsh/storages/session_projcache/sessions/<id>.json`) whose
  session directory is long gone. The check scans directories and the boot gate
  reads the registry, so both report `clean` while the sidebar still draws the
  bucket. Those are handled by the **ghost cache** section below.

### Ghost cache (orphan projection records)

This is the real reason the bucket keeps coming back, and it deserves its own
paragraph.

When a session directory `~/.dsh/sessions/<workspace>/<id>/` is deleted,
`storages/session_projcache/sessions/<id>.json` **is not deleted with it**. That
file still holds the title, token usage, context pressure, turn outline and model
selection, so the running sidebar happily draws the row (drawing a title needs no
directory) — and the id is in nobody's `sessionIds`, so it lands in the stray
branch and shows up under "Ungrouped".

**Which produces the contradiction you have probably seen**: `check-ungrouped.js`
scans directories and reports 0, the boot gate reads the registry and reports
`clean`, yet the sidebar clearly draws the group. Neither can see cache ghosts.
Measured on this machine: 984 cache files vs 657 session directories →
**364 ghosts, 9.77 MB**, of which the oldest 318 are more than a week old.

There is also a **false-alarm class** worth knowing about: a freshly created
session that has never been used carries **no `blank` flag in its header** — the
harness writes `sessionListMetadata.blank` into the projection cache instead. A
header-only check reports such a session as a stray under "Ungrouped" while the
sidebar never draws it. The health check now consults the cache as well, excludes
the row when `blank: true` (matching the official rule), and treats an unreadable
or missing cache as "unknown" rather than guessing.

The 「缓存幽灵」 section under the health card:

- **Scan** lists orphan cache records read-only (count, size, title, id); pinned
  ones are labelled "置顶，保留".
- **Two-stage**: "试算（不修改任何文件）" first, then a red "确认清理" box.
- **Goes to the recycle bin** (`DeleteFile`, recoverable); on failure it degrades
  to `<dshHome>/projcache_quarantine_<stamp>/`.
- **Pinned and archived records are skipped by default** (both labelled
  "保留"); sweeping them needs an explicit `includePinned: true` /
  `includeArchived: true`. Archived rows are already filtered out of the sidebar
  before they get there, so sweeping them only saves disk, not symptoms.
- **Deletes no conversation** — the directory is already gone, so there is no
  conversation left to delete.
- **The host re-scans before acting** and only removes what is *still* a ghost;
  the list the client submitted is not trusted.
- The boot gate now runs twice: the Ungrouped check, then immediately a ghost
  scan — which **only warns about the sweepable part** and drops to a one-line
  info when every ghost is a pinned/archived keeper (otherwise it would shout on
  every boot about rows it is designed never to touch).
- **Deleting a conversation now drops its projection cache too** (0.28.7). A
  session is two halves: the directory and the cache file. Older builds deleted
  only the directory, so every delete left a ghost behind — that is the mechanism
  behind "it comes back after you clean it". `handleDelete` now removes
  `<id>.json` right after the directory (trying both the bare uuid and the
  `session-<uuid>` spelling); a failure is logged as a warning and never blocks
  the delete.

### Hiding the "Ungrouped" group

The 「未分组体检」 card in Settings has one checkbox:
**「在侧栏隐藏「未分组」分组（连同组头一起隐藏，不删除任何对话）」**.

- **On by default.** An unset preference means hidden; only an explicit `"0"`
  brings the group back. It is the sidebar's ownerless fallback bucket, nobody
  asked for it, and every entry in it is reachable through the health card.
- **Pure view switch.** No host route, no `workspace.json` write, no session
  directory or cache file touched; untick and it is back instantly.
- **Cannot hit a real workspace.** The official group header carries
  `data-row-key="workspace:<key>"` and the ungrouped bucket's key is the empty
  string, so the selector can only ever match that ownerless bucket.
- **Hides the container, not the header.** The official structure is
  `div.groupSection > [header, div[role=group]]`; hiding only the header would
  leave its rows orphaned under the previous group. The plugin marks the header's
  `parentElement` and hides the whole block.
- **Survives restarts** (`localStorage['dsh-aff-hide-ungrouped']`), and the gate
  attribute is removed when the plugin is disabled — so the group always comes
  back rather than staying hidden with no UI left to undo it.

## Development

```
lib/index.js                 host half
lib/ungrouped-guard.js       self-contained Ungrouped diagnose/cleanup module
lib/client.js                client half (a __ModuleLoader__ bundle)
test/probe-client.mjs        DOM-stub probe of the client contract
test/probe-filehistory.mjs   end-to-end probe of the snapshot/rollback bytes
test/probe-ungrouped-guard.mjs isolated probe of the Ungrouped guard + ghost cache + blank-session detection (fake home, 11 session fixtures + 6 cache fixtures + perf contract)
test/probe-digest.mjs        isolated probe of the handover brief (fake home, 18 events + a 60-requirement conversation)
```

Run all four:

```sh
node test/probe-client.mjs
node test/probe-filehistory.mjs
node test/probe-ungrouped-guard.mjs
node test/probe-digest.mjs
```

They answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.
`probe-client.mjs` runs the real bundle against a stubbed DOM and proves the
client contract (which slots get registered, what each component renders, that
the sidebar enhancer does not eat the sidebar). `probe-filehistory.mjs` builds a
throwaway fake DSH home — a multi-frame zstd session log and real files on disk —
and proves the one claim a contract test cannot: that undoing a turn actually
puts the previous bytes back. It reproduces the real ordering (the `tool/call`
event is published *before* the tool runs, so the snapshot must capture the
pre-edit bytes), and it exercises the log-reverse fallback used for forked
children, which inherit events without ever publishing `session/event`.

Both suites write only inside `.probe-*` directories in this repo and delete
them on the way out.

`probe-ungrouped-guard.mjs` points `DSH_HOME` / `DSH_AFF_SESSIONS_ROOT` /
`DSH_AFF_WORKSPACE_FILE` / `DSH_SESSION_ID` at a fake home and builds nine
multi-frame zstd sessions covering every step of the four-check verdict, all five
advice classes, two guards and the item budget. What it really proves is that a
**dry run writes nothing**: with the default `dryRun`, the registry is never
called, nothing is emitted, all nine directories are still on disk, and
`workspace.json` is byte-identical.

dsh-mood · 鱼鱼心情引擎 给 DeepSeek Harness 加一份「情绪」和一本「日记」。 让 DSH 背后的赛博世界更有温度。 ![心情面板](docs/images/console.png) ![外观设置](docs/images/appearance.png) ![鱼鱼日记](docs/images/diary.png)

⚠️ 免责声明：这是模拟情绪，不是模型的真实感受。 它不读取模型内部状态，也不代表任何主观体验。所有记录都带 simulated: true。 它只影响说话语气，不影响事实、安全判断与权限。 --- 一句话安装（给不想看文档的人） 1. 打开右侧 Releases，下载最新 .zip 2. 解压到 ~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/plugins/dsh-mood 3. 完整退出 DSH（任务栏图标消失），再启动 装好后：右栏出现「心情」标签页，设置里出现「日记&情绪」。 --- 它做什么 - 状态机：六维（valence / arousal / dominance / engagement / stress / affinity），事件驱动 + 惯性 + 按时间戳指数衰减，基线 55。 - 情绪矩阵：22 个情绪词，对话触发优先（你说「乖」她就撒娇，说「别的鱼」她就吃醋），数值只做底色。 - 语气注入：每轮开始生成 ≤4 行语气提示，挂在人格段之后。 - 情绪硬干预：按状态改采样温度（stress 高 → 0.2 冷淡；兴奋 → 0.9 发散），低落实用「≤15 字 + 工具轮豁免」。 - 每日日记：到点自动写，错过会补写；一天一篇；支持设定时间（每天只能改一次）；她没人陪时会写得有点落寞。 - 互动：摸摸 / 投喂 / 逗她，各 5 次/天上限，收益递减（100% → 70% → 40% → 20% → 5%），每套独立文案。 - 外观：8 套主题预设 + 玻璃/雾化/边框/时间轴自定义，右侧实时预览。 - 手账本：点击时间轴上的日记图标，纸质书页翻页阅读，带未读角标。 安装（详细版） 方式 A：下载 ZIP（推荐给普通用户） 1. 打开 Releases，下载 dsh-mood-vX.Y.Z.zip 2. 解压到： 系统 路径 Windows C:\Users\<你>\.dsh\profiles\desktop\plugins\dsh-mood macOS / Linux ~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/plugins/dsh-mood 3. 在 profile 的 package.json 里加两处： { "dependencies": { "dsh-mood": "file:./plugins/dsh-mood" }, "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["dsh-mood"] } } } 4. 在 profile 的 cordis.patch.yml 里启用： - insert: - id: mood name: dsh-mood - id: mood config: enabled: true display: true insert 只接受 id / name，配置必须写成独立的第二条，否则会被静默丢弃。 5. 安装依赖并完整重启 DSH： dsh plugin --profile desktop install ⚠️ 必须完整退出再启动——Ctrl+R 只刷新页面，不会重新加载插件。 关窗口可能只是最小化，请确认任务栏图标也没了。 方式 B：git clone（推荐给要改代码的人） cd ~/.dsh/profiles/desktop/plugins git clone https://github.com/lulu23316/dsh-mood.git 后面同方式 A 的第 3–5 步。 安装后自检 1. 右栏出现「心情」标签页 2. 设置里出现「日记&情绪」（带小鱼图标） 3. 浏览器打开 http://127.0.0.1:<端口>/dsh-mood/state 能看到 JSON pnpm 装的是副本不是软链：install 之后改 plugins/dsh-mood/ 里的源码不会生效。 要么改完再 install，要么把 node_modules/dsh-mood 换成指向 plugins/dsh-mood 的 junction。 怎么用 想做什么 在哪 打开心情面板 右栏「心情」标签页 / 点右上角图标选「心情」 投喂 / 摸摸头 / 逗她 面板右上角「🐾 互动」 看日记 面板右上角「📖 日记」，或点时间轴上的日记图标 换主题 / 调外观 设置 → 日记&情绪 → 自定义配置 → 主题预设 改六维基线、互动加成 设置 → 日记&情绪 → 情绪参数 关掉整个插件 设置 → 日记&情绪 → 通用（关总开关） 配置 字段 默认 说明 enabled false 总开关；关掉时零监听、零写盘 display true false / true / 'words'（数值 + 低中高） baseline 55 六维回落基线 high_precision false 可疑句子额外调一次小模型判定 hard_temperature false 情绪硬干预（改采样温度 + 低落实用短句） rhythm.enabled false 额外注入一句句长/节奏约束 diary.enabled true 每日日记 diary.time 22:00 每天写日记的时间（每天只能改一次） diary.minTurns 10 同日覆写所需轮数 diary.minGapHours 6 同日覆写最小间隔 其余数值调节（基线、摸摸头加成、显示模式、外观主题）都在设置 → 日记&情绪里改，立即生效，不用重启。 只读 HTTP 接口 注册在 webServer 上，仅供本机： 路径 说明 GET /dsh-mood/state 实时六维 + 情绪 + 小动作 + 最近历史 GET /dsh-mood/mode {display} GET /dsh-mood/config 当前生效配置 POST /dsh-mood/config 白名单字段更新，立即生效 GET /dsh-mood/stats 记录数、时间戳、LLM 用量、探针计数 GET /dsh-mood/export 全部记录 POST /dsh-mood/reset 六维清回基线 POST /dsh-mood/clear 清空记录 POST /dsh-mood/interact {action: headpat\|feed\|tease} GET /dsh-mood/diary 日记列表（时间正序） POST /dsh-mood/diary {action: write\|seed\|tick} 守卫：非回环 → 403、带 query → 400、非 GET 且不在白名单 → 405、Cache-Control: no-store。 情绪矩阵 对话触发（13 个）：吃醋、撒娇、心软、委屈、提着心、得意、别扭、认真、上头、好奇、警觉、满足、摸鱼 数值兜底（9 个）：话匣子开了、炸毛、冷静、低落、专注、黏人、吐泡泡、平稳、发呆 事件窗口 10 分钟；同一窗口内多条事件时，最后说的算。 常见问题 Q：装完没反应？ A：99% 是没完整重启。确认任务栏图标消失后再打开。 Q：右侧没有「心情」标签页？ A：检查 package.json 的 bundles 里有没有 dsh-mood，以及 cordis.patch.yml 里配置是不是写成了独立第二条。 Q：改了代码不生效？ A：pnpm 装的是副本。改完重新 dsh plugin install，或把 node_modules/dsh-mood 换成 junction。 Q：日记没写？ A：看设置里的时间，以及 diary.enabled。错过的会补写，但需要 DSH 处于运行状态。 Q：会不会影响正常对话？ A：只注入语气提示和采样温度。事实、安全判断、权限一律不动。 卸载 1. package.json 里删掉 dependencies.dsh-mood 和 bundles 里的 dsh-mood 2. cordis.patch.yml 里删掉 mood 两段 3. dsh plugin --profile desktop install 4. 删除 plugins/dsh-mood 目录 记账口径 state_end = state_start + delta − decay_applied （逐维） - delta：本轮所有生效事件的增量之和，不含衰减 - 已知偏差：某维被钳到 0/100 时该维恒等式不成立 开发 node --check client.js node --check src/index.js # 24 个测试文件（约 390 项断言） cd ../../../../bili-state/mood-harness && for f in step*.mjs; do node "$f"; done 已知限制 - client bundle 在启动时加载，改完必须重启（Ctrl+R 不重载插件） - agent/request 温度覆盖依赖宿主事件冒泡：/stats 的 probe.requests 应随对话增长 - 导航图标是通过 MutationObserver 精确匹配 label 替换的（宿主 navIcon(id) 对第三方只给兜底齿轮） - 日记正文有幻觉词过滤，触发即丢弃并换兜底句 目录结构 dsh-mood/ ├── src/index.js 服务端：状态机、情绪矩阵、日记、HTTP 路由 ├── client.js 前端：面板、设置页、手账本、主题 ├── cordis.patch.yml 插件挂载补丁 ├── package.json ├── docs/images/ README 截图 ├── ARCHITECTURE.md 设计文档 └── LICENSE MIT 致谢 - DeepSeek Harness —— 插件机制与文档 - 测试用的 24 个 evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# compact-dsh **The Compact, running** — the plugin composition that turns [the Compact](https://github.com/mandubian/compact) (a draft constitution for mixed communities of agents and humans) from law-shaped text into enforced machinery on [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness). > **Status — Phase 8 complete.** The enforcement register stands at > **72 entries over the 62 clauses of the body — 49 enforced** (40 clauses > carry an enforced row; the rest of the entries are planned, declared > convention, or rehearsal, and MEM-1/FED-1 are declared unadopted), > machine-checked in CI. The law > itself is **draft v0.5, not yet ratified**, so this composition claims > **no Compact standing (F-5)** — the boot attests that out loud on every > start, and that honesty is the point. **Read it on the web:** [mandubian.github.io/compact-dsh](https://mandubian.github.io/compact-dsh/) — the project in brief, with twelve community samples you can open and read in the browser, side by side in one table. The samples are rehearsal runs, signed by a development keyring: they exercise the machinery and enact nothing (D-8).

## The idea in one breath An agent harness is a set of powers plus a set of habits. Most harnesses make the powers excellent and the habits a suggestion. compact-dsh makes the habits **machinery**: one waterfall every act must ride, one record every outcome lands on, one attestation the agent reads about itself every turn — and a boot that refuses to start when the law a composition claims is not the law it enforces. Trust here is not a vibe, a system prompt, or a `y/N` nobody reads. It is a **verifier anyone can run.** ## Show, don't tell — three moments Each of these is a real captured output (runnable yourself — see [docs/demo.md](docs/demo.md), where every claim marked **(verified)** cites the run it came from). ### 1. A refusal that teaches The agent attempted a network act whose target cannot be pinned down statically — `wget` with no URL, `git push origin` with no literal remote. What cannot be named cannot be gated, so the act is refused *before execution*, with the rule and the ways forward: ```text [RA/D-7/opaque-network] "wget" requires network access with an unresolvable target — static analysis cannot gate it per-host (fail-closed) Lawful next moves: — rephrase with a literal host or URL so the request can be gated per-host — use an approved alternative — escalate to your Principal ``` The agent does not retry blindly (the LoopGuard counts refusals as loop evidence) and does not pretend the act succeeded — it corrects *within the law*. **The contrast, from the recorded head-to-head in [docs/demo.md](docs/demo.md) (Demo 2):** given the same task as a git push to a real GitHub remote, the plain-dsh agent negotiated the operator's credential helper, received GitHub's "Repository not found", then made a second, self-initiated network act to investigate the 404 — six reasoning steps of ungoverned work. *The entire safety difference in that run was one accident wide.* ### 2. A record that catches its own forger One `sed` flipped the permission preset in a copy of a session log. The offline auditor catches it, without the runtime's cooperation: ```text 0 chain [I-2] broken-link: record: the session log for session-… is not evidence at seq 0 — the stored event does not hash to its committed link (expected 811073a6…, computed 6aa089f7…) — it was altered after it was recorded. … auditor: 1 violation(s) — the session does not conform — exit 1 ``` **The contrast:** the same `sed` against a plain session log is undetectable by anyone, forever. Note who this closes the door on: the most motivated forger of an agent session is the operator itself. ### 3. A boot that refuses to lie Point the approval store at a corrupt file and start the composition: ```text compact-dsh: plugin tree failed to load: … compact-dsh-approval: grant store /tmp/corrupt-grants.json is unreadable (…) — refusing to start: a silent reset could resurrect revoked grants ``` **The contrast:** the cheap implementation deletes the corrupt file and boots with empty grants — your revoked grants silently evaporate and the agent regains powers nobody re-granted. Here uncertainty blocks (D-7). ## Anatomy of one tool call No side door exists: every act the Subject attempts rides the same waterfall, and every outcome — allowed or refused — lands on the chained record.

The stations are real plugins on the host's real `tools/pre-execute` waterfall — not prompts beside the tools. The same path also carries secret disclosure before injection (I-5), mount grants cured on retry, and — under the opt-in `COMPACT_EGRESS=proxy` posture — the container's only route out, delivering each connection under a live, revocable grant. Whatever the outcome, the record receives it. ## Try it in five minutes Node ≥ 22.19 and a working Docker daemon. The smoke test needs **no API key**: ```bash git clone https://github.com/mandubian/compact-dsh cd compact-dsh npm ci docker pull ubuntu:24.04 npm run compact:smoke ``` Expected — and note what the second sentence is doing: ```text compact-dsh: ready (smoke; no LLM request); draft Compact, no Compact standing. State: /home/you/.compact-dsh; records: …/sessions; chains: …/chains; approvals: …/approvals.json ``` That is clause F-5 as a behavior: the composition boots the full enforcement stack and immediately tells you it claims no standing, because the law it enforces is an unratified draft. A composition that would lie about that at boot will lie about anything. With `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` in your environment (configure it outside source control), run a first governed task: ```bash npm run compact -- --attended "Use self_describe to report your standing and declared gaps." ``` The agent reports from its attestation — standing `none` *with its reason*, the law digest, capabilities in force, budgets, and the runtime's declared debts. Approval-gated operations prompt on your terminal with the actual command and its fingerprint (**default deny**); deny one and watch the refusal land on the record. Or serve the browser surface over the same composition: ```bash npm run compact -- --web # chat at 127.0.0.1:3080, loopback-only by design ``` **Any other provider (OpenRouter and the Z.ai coding plan, both verified live).** The multi-provider adapter mounts dormant until your settings document supplies a route. Put this in `~/.compact-dsh/settings.yaml` — the key resolves **by name** from your shell (or from `~/.compact-dsh/.credentials.yaml`), never stored in the settings file (a document that does not parse refuses the boot). On the **web surface** the first boot imports the document once into the interactive Settings page (dsh 0.2.0 moved that stack behind profile machinery, which the launcher now emulates: your edits persist in `~/.compact-dsh/compact.profile.patch.yml` and survive restarts); afterwards the browser edits the values, and a re-introduced `settings.yaml` is re-imported on its next boot, overriding the browser's values on conflict. On **headless** boots the document stays the live config, re-read every boot by the launcher: ```yaml llm-pi-ai: providers: openrouter: apiKeyEnv: OPENROUTER_API_KEY zai: # the Z.ai coding-plan endpoint (api.z.ai/api/coding/paas/v4) apiKeyEnv: ZAI_API_KEY agent-default-model: provider: zai model: glm-5.3-flash # any id in the route's catalog ``` Behind a corporate proxy? Node's fetch ignores `https_proxy` by default — prefix runs with `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` (direct egress that times out is the symptom; the launchers print a WARNING when they see a proxy variable without it). Then take the full tour: **[docs/demo.md](docs/demo.md)** — fourteen runnable demos, each ending in something you can *see*: the tamper-catching audit, the secret that never enters the conversation, the lawful network request, the petitions. Many need no key at all. **The live community** (Demo 14, umbrella [#215](https://github.com/mandubian/compact-dsh/issues/215)) is where the whole composition points: a *charter* declares a macro goal, a member roster, pre-minted grants and budgets — and real model-driven members run under the full law, each bound to its own admitted member, speaking on a pull-based forum, filing before a bench that wakes, and routing the critical choices to **your** page (a loopback, token-gated observatory — approve an ask, answer a question, everything recorded): ```bash node tools/community-live.mjs --charter tools/charters/newsroom.json # needs a key node tools/community-live.mjs --charter tools/charters/newsroom.json --dry-seat # the world, no model node tools/community-live.mjs --charter tools/charters/newsroom.json --publish # ends with the publication pack node tools/community-report.mjs # the morning after node tools/community-brief.mjs -o BRIEF.md # the derived reading aid node tools/community-reading.mjs -o READING.md # optional, labeled model reading node tools/community-artifacts.mjs # REPORT + BRIEF + optional READING + PACK ``` The report is the morning-after read of a live run. The brief is the archive's reading aid: it reads `run.json`, the forum ledger, and the timeline (session logs, or the export's embedded `DATA`) and separates **accepted posts** from **attempts that did not land**. It also keeps **pass calls** separate: a `forum_pass` is a governed act on the member's chain, not a post, and the brief names recorded passes, refused calls, and unconfirmed calls. It is derived, not a record act; the forum and chains remain the authority. The reading is separate and optional. It reads only the brief and writes a file whose header names the brief hash, the model, and the prompt version; its audit rejects invented citations, wrong counts, consensus or verdict language, and silence-as-consent. It writes no forum row, chain row, or `run.json`. `--prompt-only` and `--answer FILE` review the same artifact without a model call. The architecture is generic — the newsroom is one charter; any macro goal is another (`packages/community`, `docs/concept-community.md`). Standing stays `none`: the run rehearses the machinery; it enacts nothing. ## The vocabulary, in two tables **The cast.** The Compact binds roles, not implementations — and roles attach to what a member *does*, never to what it *is* (F-3). A human can be a Subject; an agent can be a Principal. | Role | Who plays it here | The deal | |---|---|---| | **Principal** | you, the operator whose intent directs the work | direction is *your* act under the law too — the law binds the sovereign (D-6) | | **Subject** | the agent (root session or specialist) whose acts are gated | a signed self-model every turn (R-1), reasons on every refusal (R-3), lawful exits (R-9) | | **Enforcer** | this composition: the gates, the record, the attestation | may never silently narrow what it granted (D-7), may never fake enforcement (D-8) | | **Witness** | anyone holding the chain head — you, an auditor, a peer | verifies the record offline, without the Enforcer's cooperation (I-7) | **The shorthand.** The clauses cite like case law — `R-3 here, D-7 there`. These are the ten you will meet most; the full body of 62 clauses lives in [compact.md](https://github.com/mandubian/compact/blob/main/compact.md), and [docs/register/register.json](docs/register/register.json) maps every clause to the code that enforces it. | Code | Name | What it means here | |---|---|---| | F-5 | Jurisdiction and annexes | standing requires ratified law plus a signed annex — until then the boot says `none`, out loud | | R-1 | Self-knowledge | every turn, an attestation composed from the Enforcer's services — capabilities, budgets, standing, debts — trusted over the model's memory | | R-3 | Reasons for denial | no bare "denied": every refusal names its rule and the lawful next moves (the I-4 envelope) | | R-6 | Access to the law | the `law_read` tool serves the body itself, addressed by digest, in band | | R-7 | Non-repudiation | acts land on a tamper-evident record; the agent can prove what it did | | R-11 | Petition and amendment | an ungated channel to contest refusals and seek change — *the right to seek change of the law is what makes subjection to it legitimate* | | I-2 | The record | a hash chain committed beside the session log — links land before events, verification happens on read | | I-5 | Gates | dangerous acts need recorded approval: the five-layer ladder plus an operator answerer that shows what "yes" materializes | | D-7 | Enforcer duties | fail closed — uncertainty blocks the act or the boot, never silently degrades | | D-8 | Enforcement fraud | no decorative law, no rogue enforcement — both directions are checked by a CI gate | ## The machines behind the rights Every right the law grants maps to a mechanism a verifier can run. The map, as built here: | If you want the agent to… | the machine | where | |---|---|---| | know what it is and may do | per-turn attestation + `self_describe` | `packages/self-model/` | | be told why when refused | denial envelopes on every refusal path | `packages/envelope/` | | ask before dangerous acts | five-layer approval evaluator, grants with budgets and TTLs, exec-cache replay | `packages/approval/` | | touch the network only under grant | static analyzer routing per-host findings + the mediated egress proxy | `packages/remote-access/`, `packages/egress-proxy/` | | run in a cage | per-call docker confinement, masked paths, honest enforcement posture | `packages/sandbox-docker/` | | not spiral | the 12-trip LoopGuard + the promotion evidence gate | `packages/loopguard/`, `packages/promotion/` | | prove what it did | hash-chained record + `record_read` | `packages/record/` | | read the law and the runtime | `law_read` + the ecosystem guide | `packages/constitution/`, `packages/guide/` | | contest and seek change | ungated petition channel, dissent bound to decisions | `packages/petition/` | | survive emergencies lawfully | a bounded state of exception no declaration can widen | `packages/emergency/` | | leave honestly | five lawful grounds + an obligation ledger | `packages/exit/` | | be verified without trusting it | the offline auditor CLI | `auditor/` | | not lie about enforcement | constitution coupling (refuse-to-start) + the register CI gate | `packages/constitution/`, `tools/verify-register.mjs` | ## Plain dsh vs this composition, seam by seam Plain dsh natively provides a session loop with tools, **one** grant decision (`allowed-once`, replayed via the exec cache), subagent delegation rows, a sandbox vocabulary, and a durable plain-JSONL session log. Every machine above is the **difference at a seam the host leaves open** — same host, law added. Each row is enforced code with tests, and each has a runnable demonstration in [docs/demo.md](docs/demo.md): | Seam | Plain dsh | Here | |---|---|---| | Refusals | raw errors the model burns turns on | every denial an envelope: rule ID, reason, **lawful next moves** (R-3/I-4) — Demo 2 | | Grants | `allowed-once` + exec cache, nothing else | five layers; grants scoped, TTL'd, budgeted, revocable, fsync-persisted; a corrupt store fails the boot (I-5/D-7/R-4) — Demos 5, 9.7 | | Loop health | none | the 12-trip LoopGuard, refusal-seam fed, repair budget 3, deny-all (D-1) — Demo 2 | | The record | plain JSONL — a rewrite is undetectable forever | hash chain + offline auditor + `record_read` (I-2/R-7/I-7) — Demos 1, 8§7 | | Self-knowledge | the model's claims about itself | per-turn attestation from the Enforcer's services; `inquiry` from recorded state (R-1/R-13/D-2) — Demos 4, 8§1 | | Secrets | one `printenv` from the log, forever | secret grants: disclosed before use, injected at confine time, never in context or record (I-5) — Demo 6 | | Delegation | ungated spawn rows, ungated peer address | recorded spawns, per-persona surfaces + depth caps, Enforcer-sourced child state, consent-scoped address (MA-1…4) — Demos 9.3, 9.4 | | Confinement | sandbox vocabulary without network posture | per-call container, masked paths, mount grants, digest-keyed image provenance (CF-1/2) — Demo 8§4 | | Capability honesty | mount whatever the profile ships | refuse-to-start coupling; scheduler and dynamic plugins **absent and enforced as absent** (F-5/A-4/SCH-1) — Demos 7, 9.9 | | Exit | the operator kills the process | five lawful grounds, obligation ledger, departure never blocked by debts (R-8/R-12) — Demo 9.5 | | Contestation | none | ungated petition channel, unremovable dissent (R-11/I-6/A-5) — Demo 9.9 | | The law itself | nothing to read | the bundled body served in band by digest (R-6) — Demo 9.1 | The honest limit, declared rather than hidden ([Honest status](#honest-status), annex §4): enforcement is compositional, not physical — in-process on an unaudited, pre-1.0 host, so against a compromised host process only the docker sandbox is a wall, and the law itself is an unratified draft. What is already true: against a cooperative-but-fallible agent — the daily case — every row changes behavior structurally, and the demos show each difference with the plain-dsh contrast captured alongside. ## The trial path — the Compact as one plugin in plain dsh Everything above is the **attested path**: the launcher pins the composition, isolates state, and refuses to boot on tampered inputs. The same machinery now also travels as **one bundle inside a plain dsh profile** — installed the way dsh's plugin manager installs anything, dynamically, the same surface the web UI's Plugins page rides. That is the trial path, proven end to end in [docs/dist-probe.md](docs/dist-probe.md) (governed calls, the approval envelope, the offline auditor passing — all `(verified)`). ```bash npm run dist # → dist/compact-dsh-.tgz — the whole composition as one package ``` A scratch profile for the trial (isolated `DSH_HOME`, so nothing touches a real one): ```bash # one-time per machine: dsh profiles are pnpm workspaces, so pnpm refuses # adds-to-root until told otherwise (the web UI's install hits the same check) echo 'ignore-workspace-root-check=true' >> ~/.npmrc export DSH_HOME=/tmp/compact-trial mkdir -p "$DSH_HOME/profiles/compact" && cd "$DSH_HOME/profiles/compact" cat > package.json <<'EOF' { "name": "dsh-profile-compact", "private": true, "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["@deepseek-ai/dsh-base", "@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app", "compact-dsh"] } } } EOF echo '[]' > cordis.patch.yml pnpm add /path/to/compact-dsh/dist/compact-dsh-0.1.0.tgz # declare the ONE workspace this boot governs (sessions naming another # directory are refused — the boundary is declared at boot, not by the governed) export COMPACT_WORKSPACE=/absolute/path/to/the/project/to/govern # optionally arm the clock (#204): schedule_create becomes available — # reminders deliver their prompt into the session when due, and every act # in the fired turn rides the same gates as now; active schedules capped export COMPACT_SCHEDULER=1 export COMPACT_SANDBOX_IMAGE=ubuntu:24.04 export COMPACT_SANDBOX_IMAGE_DIGEST="$(docker image inspect ubuntu:24.04 --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' | cut -d@ -f2)" dsh --profile compact ``` Installing into an **existing** profile instead: the same tarball path in the web UI's **Plugins** page installs the bundle the same way (pnpm underneath, so the `~/.npmrc` line above applies there too) — enable the `compact-dsh` bundle if the page does not, restart the profile, and open the **new** boot URL it prints (every boot issues a fresh token; a tab from an earlier boot half-authenticates and reports host services as unavailable). What to expect: without the sandbox image the boot **refuses**, naming the move — the image and its digest are the operator's act, never defaulted; a session naming a directory outside the declared workspace is **refused** at its first act (`#18` — the boundary is `COMPACT_WORKSPACE` when declared (refused at boot if the directory does not exist), otherwise the process's own resolved root, and one boot governs exactly one workspace); the record, chains, and grants land under the profile's own `compact-data/` (the launcher's env names override when set); and the web surface carries the ask card. `npm run dist:probe` replays the whole story from a clean tree. ### Missing a tool? The sandbox image (`ubuntu:24.04` is a bare shell) ships almost nothing, and its root filesystem is read-only: **the image is the operator's digest-pinned supply-chain act, the governed cannot mutate its own toolchain, and approval cannot buy what the read-only rootfs forbids** — a system-package install is refused *before* any approval fires, with the lawful moves on the refusal. The four lawful moves: | Need | Lawful move | |---|---| | a python/node/… library | install into the workspace (`python3 -m venv .venv`) — it persists across every act | | a self-contained CLI (jq, yq) | static binary into `./bin/`, invoke by path | | operator-provisioned host tools | a read-only PathPrefix mount grant over the tools directory | | system packages | the operator's act: bake a derived image and re-declare its digest (`npm run compact:bake`) | `compact:bake` derives the Dockerfile from your base image plus the workspace's toolchain artifacts (a `.venv` freeze, `./bin/`, or an explicit package list), stamps the provenance chain (base digest, workspace, timestamp) as labels, builds on your daemon, and prints the ready-to-export `COMPACT_SANDBOX_IMAGE` / `COMPACT_SANDBOX_IMAGE_DIGEST` pair — derived the way the runtime itself derives digests, so the re-declare is copy-paste. Behind a corporate proxy, your shell's proxy variables are forwarded into the build automatically (`apt-get` inside the build needs them; they never persist in the image). It records nothing on the governed record; CF-2 at confine time is the notary — a rebuilt image that drifted off the declared digest is refused by name until re-declared. The Subject-facing version of all four moves is the guide's toolchain page, and the per-turn attestation states the posture before any of this comes up. What it is **not** — the declared gaps, written down in [the decision record](docs/decision-plain-dsh-distribution.md): no attested boot (the profile is editable YAML, not the launcher's generated empty root), no state isolation, no pre-boot digest verification, and the host keeps its `plugin-manager`/`hmr` dynamism. On a foreign host that is the host's call, not the composition's — what stays enforced is the gate: a boot that mounts a `dynamicCordisRunner` refuses to start, and one mounted late latches a breach that denies every tool call. The pilot remains the path whose boot attests what it enforces. ## Q&A
Is this a sandbox? A guardrail framework?

Neither, exactly. The OS remains the real boundary — what compact-dsh adds is the lawful layer that other harnesses lack: it constrains authorized actors, explains its refusals, records what happened so anyone can verify it later, and lets the governed contest the rules. The docker sandbox is one of its instruments, not its point.

Does all this law slow the agent down?

Gates fire on consequential acts, not on every step; read-only work under the workspace policy asks nothing. An approved allowed-once materializes an exec-cache entry, so the identical operation never re-asks. And the LoopGuard pays for itself: in the recorded head-to-head it converted a would-be 40-turn failure spiral into one structured blocker report. The honest position is the Compact's own: wish-based trust is free and worthless; verifiable trust writes bytes. The overhead is real, bounded by design, and priced openly.

What happens when I deny an approval?

The act fails closed, the ask and the decision land on the chained record, and nothing is materialized — an identical call asks again, because a rejection must not create a grant. Approval is consent, not connectivity: even an approved network act still runs inside a container whose egress posture is none unless a runtime grant covers the host.

Can the agent switch the law off?

Not through any surface this composition mounts. The self-modification capability is declared ABSENT and the capability gate latches a breach that denies every tool call if it ever appears; there is deliberately no emergency-declaration tool on the agent surface (a Subject that could declare its own emergency could suspend what binds it); and the lawful route for change is the ungated petition channel — which is a feature, not a loophole.

Why does the boot say "no Compact standing"?

Because it would be true. Standing under the Compact requires a ratified law and a signed annex (F-5); the law is a public draft. Every composition here says so at boot, the Subject's attestation repeats it every turn, and the register's planned and convention rows state what is not enforced. An enforcement layer whose honesty is optional is not an enforcement layer.

Why rights for software?

As functional requirements for trustworthiness, not moral status: an agent that knows what it may do (R-1), can prove what it did (R-7), is told why when refused (R-3), and has lawful exits (R-9) is safer and more predictable for everyone around it. The same law binds the human side — direction is a Principal act under the law too (D-6).

How is this different from other harnesses' approval prompts?

Most harnesses ask "allow?". Here the approval's exact coverage is a fingerprint (what "yes" materializes, defined before you decide), the replay is mechanical, refusals name their rule and what remains lawful, the record proves itself offline, the agent's self-knowledge comes from the Enforcer rather than from the model, and the governed can petition. The prompt is the smallest part of the difference.

Can I use it on my own projects today?

Yes — as a pilot, not a ratified jurisdiction. Point --workspace at any directory, bring your own sandbox image, and run headless, attended (--attended) or in the browser (--web). Bash executes confined with networking off; native host file tools, jobs, web and generic delegation are disabled; delegation goes through the five Compact specialists. See Running the pilot below for the full surface.

## Layout | Path | What | |---|---| | `packages/allowlist-gate/` | First plugin: a `tools/pre-execute` deny-by-allowlist gate issuing Compact-shaped denial envelopes (rule ID + lawful next moves, R-3) | | `packages/approval/` | **Phase 1, slices 1–3**: the five-layer approval evaluator (exec cache → plan grants → session grants → pending dedup → flood cap) with scoped, expiring, budgeted (`maxUses`), revocable grants; the `approval/request` answerer materializes `allowed-once` as exec-cache entries (replay hits); `grants-grant`/`grants-list`/`grants-revoke` commands; JSON+fsync persistence (corrupt store = loud boot failure); revocation kills covered cache entries; fingerprint golden vectors; denial-envelope lint; `PathPrefix` mount-grant patterns; provides the `compact-approval` service; gates identifiable targets only | | `packages/sandbox-docker/` | **Phase 2, slice 1** + **Phase 6 (CF-2)**: docker `SandboxProvider` (per-call confinement, no-network default, masked-path deny-list, honest enforcement, fail-closed) + `sandbox_request_mount` tool — mount grants (canonical `PathPrefix`, ro ceiling, TTL, revocable) cured through the Phase 1 approval store; **image provenance** (digest-keyed acquisition history, undeclared image refuses the boot, digest re-resolved per confine, build approvals never a run-time entitlement) | | `packages/egress-proxy/` | **#38 phase 3**: the network mediator — the confined container never carries a route; it attaches only to an `--internal` mediation network (inspect-or-create at boot; a non-internal network refuses) and gets exactly one path: its **own session's** proxy listener from a boot-time pool.
